maths_aqa_f.2.0.summary: Compound units combine two or more standard units to describe a relationship, such as speed (distance/time) or density (mass/volume). Converting between standard and compound units requires careful attention to the units involved, ensuring that the numerator and denominator are in compatible forms before performing calculations. This skill is essential for real-world applications like calculating travel times, fuel efficiency, and material properties.

core.p: A compound unit is formed by dividing one standard unit by another. It describes a rate or a relationship between two different physical quantities. For example, speed is distance divided by time. Understanding the structure of the unit is the first step in any conversion or calculation.
bullets: Standard units: metres (m), seconds (s), kilograms (kg), litres (L).
Compound units: metres per second (m/s), kilometres per hour (km/h), kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).
The slash '/' or the word 'per' indicates division.
The unit before 'per' is the numerator (top); the unit after is the denominator (bottom).

callouts.p: A unit that is formed by combining two or more standard units, typically using division (e.g., m/s).

core.p: Speed is the most common compound unit in GCSE Maths. It tells you how fast an object is moving. The formula is Speed = Distance / Time. To convert between units, you must ensure the distance and time units match the desired speed unit.
bullets: Common units: m/s (metres per second) and km/h (kilometres per hour).
To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6 (since 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h).
To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6 (since 1 km/h = 0.278 m/s).
Always check if the question asks for the answer in a specific unit.

callouts.p: 1 km/h = 1000 m / 3600 s = 5/18 m/s. Therefore, to convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.

core.p: Converting between m/s and km/h is a frequent exam question. The key is to understand the relationship between metres and kilometres, and seconds and hours. 1 km = 1000 m and 1 hour = 3600 seconds.
bullets: Step 1: Convert the distance unit (km to m or m to km).
Step 2: Convert the time unit (h to s or s to h).
Step 3: Divide the new distance by the new time.

callouts.p: Do not just multiply by 1000. You must account for both the distance and time changes.

core.p: Density measures how much mass is packed into a given volume. It is calculated as Density = Mass / Volume. Common units are kg/m³ and g/cm³. Converting between these units requires attention to the cubic nature of volume.
bullets: To convert kg/m³ to g/cm³, divide by 1000.
Example: 1000 kg/m³ = 1000000 g / 1000000 cm³ = 1 g/cm³.

callouts.p: The mass per unit volume of a substance. Formula: Density = Mass / Volume.

core.p: Pressure is the force applied per unit area. It is measured in Pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². To calculate pressure, divide the force in Newtons by the area in square metres.
bullets: Formula: Pressure = Force / Area.
Force is measured in Newtons (N).
Area is measured in square metres (m²).
If area is given in cm², convert to m² by dividing by 10,000.

callouts.p: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². Therefore, to convert cm² to m², divide by 10,000.

core.p: Rates of pay are often given as an hourly rate. To find total earnings, multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked. If the rate is given per week, convert to per hour by dividing by the number of working hours in a week.
bullets: Hourly Rate = Total Pay / Hours Worked.
Total Pay = Hourly Rate * Hours Worked.
If a weekly rate is given, divide by 40 (standard working week) to get the hourly rate.
Overtime may be paid at a different rate (e.g., time and a half).

callouts.p: Always check if the question specifies a standard working week (usually 40 hours) if converting weekly to hourly rates.

core.p: Unit pricing is a compound unit used to compare the cost of different amounts of a product. It is calculated as Price / Quantity. This allows you to determine which product offers better value for money.
bullets: Formula: Unit Price = Total Price / Quantity.
Common units: £/kg, p/100ml, £/litre.
To compare, ensure both products are converted to the same unit (e.g., both in £/kg).
The lower unit price indicates better value.

callouts.p: Do not compare total prices directly if the quantities are different. Always calculate the unit price.

core.p: When converting compound units, follow a systematic approach. Identify the starting unit and the target unit. Convert the numerator and denominator separately to compatible standard units, then perform the division.
bullets: Identify the starting unit (e.g., km/h).
Identify the target unit (e.g., m/s).
Convert the numerator (km to m).
Convert the denominator (h to s).
Divide the new numerator by the new denominator.

callouts.p: Use estimation to check if your answer is reasonable. For example, 100 km/h is roughly 28 m/s.

core.p: Compound units are used extensively in real life. Speed limits are in km/h, fuel efficiency in miles per gallon, and material density in kg/m³. Understanding these units helps in making informed decisions and solving practical problems.
bullets: Speed limits: km/h or mph.
Fuel efficiency: miles per gallon (mpg) or litres per 100 km.
Material selection: Density determines if a material is suitable for a specific application.
Pressure: Used in engineering and medicine (e.g., blood pressure in mmHg).

callouts.p: Always consider the context when choosing the appropriate unit. For example, use m/s for scientific calculations and km/h for everyday driving.

core.p: Students often make errors in unit conversion by forgetting to convert both the numerator and denominator. Another common mistake is using the wrong formula for the compound unit. Always double-check your units and formulas.
bullets: Forgetting to convert time from hours to seconds when calculating speed in m/s.
Using the wrong formula (e.g., Speed = Time / Distance instead of Distance / Time).
Confusing kg/m³ with g/cm³ without applying the correct conversion factor.
Not checking if the final answer is in the required unit.

callouts.p: If you forget to convert the time unit, your speed will be off by a factor of 3600.

core.p: Memorize the key formulas for compound units. Speed = Distance / Time, Density = Mass / Volume, Pressure = Force / Area. These formulas are the foundation for all calculations involving compound units.
bullets: Speed: S = D / T
Density: ρ = m / V
Pressure: P = F / A
Rate of Pay: R = E / H

callouts.p: A visual aid to help remember the relationship between the three variables in a formula. Cover the variable you want to find.

analogy.t: Compound units are like a recipe's ingredients per serving.
analogy.p: Just as a recipe tells you how much flour (mass) is needed per cup (volume) to make a cake, density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. If you change the serving size (volume), you must adjust the amount of flour (mass) accordingly. Similarly, when converting units, you are adjusting the 'serving size' of your measurement to match the required format.

terms.d: A unit formed by combining two or more standard units, typically using division.
The rate at which an object covers distance. Formula: Speed = Distance / Time.
The mass per unit volume of a substance. Formula: Density = Mass / Volume.
The force applied per unit area. Formula: Pressure = Force / Area.
The SI unit of pressure, defined as 1 Newton per square metre (N/m²).
The cost per unit of a product, used to compare value for money.
The top part of a fraction or compound unit, representing the quantity being divided.
The bottom part of a fraction or compound unit, representing the quantity by which the numerator is divided.
A number used to convert one unit to another, such as 1000 for converting km to m.
The amount of money earned per unit of time, such as per hour or per week.
The amount of space occupied by a substance, measured in cubic units (e.g., m³, cm³).
A push or pull upon an object, measured in Newtons (N).
The amount of space inside a two-dimensional shape, measured in square units (e.g., m², cm²).
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg) or grams (g).
The length of the path between two points, measured in metres (m) or kilometres (km).
The duration of an event, measured in seconds (s), minutes (min), or hours (h).

mistakes.w: Converting km/h to m/s by multiplying by 1000 only.
mistakes.r: Must convert both km to m (x1000) and h to s (x3600), then divide.

mistakes.w: Using Speed = Time / Distance.
mistakes.r: Correct formula is Speed = Distance / Time.

mistakes.w: Confusing kg/m³ with g/cm³ without conversion.
mistakes.r: 1 kg/m³ = 0.001 g/cm³. Must divide by 1000 to convert.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert cm² to m² when calculating pressure.
mistakes.r: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². Must divide area in cm² by 10,000 to get m².

mistakes.w: Comparing total prices instead of unit prices for value for money.
mistakes.r: Must calculate price per unit (e.g., £/kg) to compare fairly.

mistakes.w: Using the wrong conversion factor for time (e.g., 60 instead of 3600 for hours to seconds).
mistakes.r: 1 hour = 3600 seconds. Must multiply by 3600, not 60.

mistakes.w: Not checking if the final answer is in the required unit.
mistakes.r: Always read the question carefully and ensure the answer is in the specified unit.

exam.q: Convert 54 km/h to m/s.
exam.tip: Remember to convert both distance and time.

exam.q: A car travels 120 km in 1.5 hours. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
exam.tip: Convert units before dividing.

exam.q: The mass of a metal block is 2.5 kg and its volume is 0.001 m³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
exam.tip: Convert mass to grams and volume to cm³.

exam.q: A force of 500 N is applied to an area of 0.5 m². Calculate the pressure in Pa.
exam.tip: Ensure force is in Newtons and area is in m².

exam.q: A product costs £12 for 3 kg. Another costs £15 for 4 kg. Which is better value for money?
exam.tip: Calculate unit price for both products.

exam.q: A worker earns £400 for a 40-hour week. Calculate their hourly rate.
exam.tip: Divide total pay by total hours.

exam.q: Convert 20 m/s to km/h.
exam.tip: Multiply by 3.6 to convert m/s to km/h.

exam.q: A gas has a mass of 5 g and a volume of 2 L. Calculate its density in kg/m³.
exam.tip: Convert grams to kg and litres to m³.

worked.q: A train travels 180 km in 2 hours. What is its speed in m/s?
steps: Convert distance: 180 km = 180,000 m
Convert time: 2 h = 7200 s
Calculate speed: 180,000 / 7200 = 25 m/s

worked.q: A metal cube has a mass of 800 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density in kg/m³?
steps: Convert mass: 800 g = 0.8 kg
Convert volume: 100 cm³ = 0.0001 m³
Calculate density: 0.8 / 0.0001 = 8000 kg/m³

worked.q: A force of 200 N is applied to an area of 0.05 m². What is the pressure in Pa?
steps: Use formula: Pressure = Force / Area
Calculate: 200 / 0.05 = 4000 Pa

maths_aqa_f.2.1.summary: A scale drawing represents a real object or region proportionally by altering all dimensions using a fixed ratio or scale factor. On maps and blueprints, scales are presented either as statements such as **1 cm to 5 km** or unitless ratios like **1 : 25 000**. Mastering scale requires converting accurately between metric units, multiplying or dividing by scale factors, and measuring physical lines with precision using a standard ruler.

core.p: A **scale diagram** is a mathematically accurate drawing where every length is proportional to the real-world length it represents. Scale allows us to represent huge structures, such as towns, landscapes, or buildings, on a single sheet of paper.
bullets: **Scale** defines the exact ratio comparing drawing lengths to actual real-world lengths.
All measurements are scaled by the **same factor** to maintain correct shape and proportion.
A scale drawing that is smaller than the real object is a **reduction**.
A scale drawing that is larger than the real object (e.g., microscopic cells) is an **enlargement**.

callouts.p: A drawing that represents a real object with accurately reduced or enlarged lengths using a constant proportional factor.
If one wall on a blueprint is halved in length, every single wall and feature on that blueprint must also be halved.

core.p: Exams present scales in two main formats: **word statements** (e.g., 1 cm represents 2 metres) and **ratios** (e.g., 1 : 200). Understanding how to work with both forms is essential for Foundation Tier success.
bullets: **Word Statement Scale**: Specifies unit explicit conversions, such as **1 cm to 5 km**.
**Ratio Scale**: Written without units as **1 : n**, meaning 1 unit on the map equals **n** of the *same* units in reality.
A ratio of **1 : 100** means 1 cm on paper represents 100 cm (which equals 1 metre) in real life.
Ratio scales work with any unit: 1 mm on paper equals 100 mm in reality.

head: Scale Format
Example
Meaning on Paper
rows: Every 1 cm measured on drawing = 4 metres in real life
Every 1 unit measured on drawing = 50 units in real life
1 cm on map = 25 000 cm (250 metres) in real life

callouts.p: When a ratio has no units given, both sides of the ratio always use identical units.

core.p: Scale problems almost always require converting between **millimetres (mm)**, **centimetres (cm)**, **metres (m)**, and **kilometres (km)**. Mistakes on unit conversions are the most common reason students lose marks.
bullets: **1 cm = 10 mm** (Multiply cm by 10 to get mm; divide mm by 10 to get cm).
**1 m = 100 cm** (Multiply m by 100 to get cm; divide cm by 100 to get m).
**1 km = 1000 m** (Multiply km by 1000 to get m; divide m by 1000 to get km).
To go directly from **cm to km**, divide by **100 000** (100 x 1000).

callouts.p: Do not mix up metres and kilometres! 1 km is 1000 metres, NOT 100 metres.

core.h: 4. Calculating Real Distances from Map Measurements
core.p: To find a real-world distance from a map measurement, you **multiply** the measured length on the drawing by the scale value, then convert to suitable real-world units (m or km).
bullets: Step 1: Measure the distance accurately on the drawing in centimetres using a ruler.
Step 2: Multiply this measurement by the scale multiplier.
Step 3: Convert the resulting total into metres or kilometres as requested.
Example: Map distance = 6 cm. Scale is **1 cm to 3 km**. Real distance = 6 x 3 = **18 km**.

callouts.p: Drawing Distance to Real Distance = MULTIPLY by scale factor.

core.h: 5. Calculating Map Distances from Real Distances
core.p: To find how long a line should be drawn on paper when given a real-world distance, you **divide** the real distance by the scale factor.
bullets: Step 1: Ensure the real-world distance is in the unit required by the scale (e.g., metres or kilometres).
Step 2: Divide the real distance by the scale amount.
Step 3: State the final answer clearly in centimetres or millimetres as instructed.
Example: Real length = 45 m. Scale is **1 cm to 5 m**. Drawing length = 45 ÷ 5 = **9 cm**.

callouts.p: Real Distance to Drawing Distance = DIVIDE by scale factor.

core.p: AQA examiners frequently ask students to express a given scale statement as a ratio in the form **1 : n**. The crucial rule is that both sides must be in the **same units** before removing the units.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the statement scale, e.g., **1 cm to 2 m**.
Step 2: Convert the larger unit so both sides share the same unit: **1 cm to 200 cm**.
Step 3: Remove the units to express as a ratio: **1 : 200**.
Step 4: Ensure the left-hand number is simplified to **1**.

callouts.p: A scale ratio where 1 unit on the drawing represents n of the identical unit in real life.
Writing 1 cm to 2 m as 1 : 2 without converting metres to centimetres is incorrect!

core.h: 7. Finding an Unknown Scale Factor from Measurements
core.p: If you are given both a drawing length and the corresponding real length, you can calculate the scale factor or ratio by dividing the real length by the drawing length in matching units.
bullets: Step 1: Convert both measurements to identical units (usually centimetres).
Step 2: Divide the real distance by the map distance to find **n**.
Step 3: Write the ratio as **1 : n**.
Example: Map distance = 4 cm, Real distance = 80 m (8000 cm). n = 8000 ÷ 4 = 2000. Scale ratio = **1 : 2000**.

callouts.p: Always double check: Is the real object much larger than the drawing? If yes, n in 1 : n must be greater than 1.

core.p: In AQA exam papers, you will be expected to use a physical ruler to measure distances on printed diagrams. Precision is critical; mark schemes typically allow a tolerance of only **±2 mm**.
bullets: Measure from the exact center of point/cross A to the center of point/cross B.
Align the 0 mm mark of your ruler precisely with the starting point.
Read measurements in millimetres or centimetres to 1 decimal place (e.g. 7.4 cm).
Double-check your ruler alignment before performing scale multiplication.

callouts.p: Make sure you do not start measuring from the physical edge of the ruler—start at the zero mark!

core.h: 9. Scale Diagrams with Bearings and Directions
core.p: Scale map questions on Foundation papers often incorporate basic compass directions or **three-figure bearings** to locate places on a grid or map.
bullets: Combine scale calculations with measuring angles clockwise from North.
Step 1: Calculate map distance from real distance using scale.
Step 2: Measure the bearing angle from North using a protractor.
Step 3: Draw the line along the correct angle at the precise calculated length.

callouts.p: Bearings are always measured clockwise from North and written using 3 digits (e.g., 045°).

core.h: 10. Linear Scale Factor in Geometric Enlargement
core.p: Scale factors are also used when enlarging 2D geometric shapes. The **linear scale factor (LSF)** is the multiplier that scales every side length of the original shape to create the enlarged image.
bullets: **Linear Scale Factor = New Side Length ÷ Corresponding Original Side Length**.
If scale factor = 3, every side length is multiplied by 3.
Angles in scaled/enlarged shapes **do not change**; the shapes remain similar.
If scale factor is fractional (e.g., 1/2), the shape shrinks in size.

callouts.p: The constant multiplier used to scale all linear dimensions of a shape.

core.h: 11. Practical Applications: Maps and Architectural Floor Plans
core.p: Questions on scale frequently use real-world contexts such as garden design plans, house floor plans, or hiking maps.
bullets: Architectural plans commonly use scales like **1 : 50** or **1 : 100**.
OS Maps (Ordnance Survey) commonly use **1 : 25 000** or **1 : 50 000**.
1 : 25 000 means **4 cm on the map = 1 km on the ground**.
1 : 50 000 means **2 cm on the map = 1 km on the ground**.

callouts.p: Memorising that 1 cm on a 1 : 25 000 map is 250 m allows for rapid mental checks during exams.

analogy.p: Think of scale factor like zooming in or out with a camera lens. When you zoom out, an entire mountain range fits onto a tiny 10 cm phone screen, but every peak, tree, and valley retains its exact proportional relationship to everything else. If a tree is twice as tall as a cabin in real life, it will be twice as tall on your screen. The scale factor is the multiplier that bridges your tiny phone screen measurement to the actual mountain range. This analogy breaks down if the lens distorts the edges (fisheye effect), whereas mathematical scale factor is always perfectly uniform across every direction.

terms.d: The ratio of a length on a drawing or map to the actual corresponding length in reality.
The number that all side lengths of a shape or diagram are multiplied by to calculate enlarged or reduced lengths.
A ratio written in the form 1 : n that compares map distance to real-world distance in identical units.
A representation of a real-life object or region drawn accurately using a specific scale factor.
The measured length between two points directly on paper or a printed map.
The actual physical distance between two locations on the ground or on an object.
The constant multiplier applied to lengths when enlarging or reducing 2D geometric shapes.
A relationship between two quantities where increasing one causes the other to increase by the same multiplicative factor.
A numerical value used to multiply or divide a quantity when converting from one measurement unit to another.
Standard metric unit of length equivalent to 100 centimetres.
Standard metric unit of distance equivalent to 1000 metres or 100 000 centimetres.
Standard metric unit of length equivalent to 10 millimetres.
A scale drawing showing a view from above of the layout of rooms in a building.
A direction measured in degrees clockwise from due North, written as a 3-digit number.

mistakes.w: Writing 1 cm to 5 km as the ratio 1 : 5
mistakes.r: Convert km to cm first! 5 km = 500 000 cm, so the correct scale ratio is 1 : 500 000.

mistakes.w: Multiplying real distance by scale factor to find map length
mistakes.r: To find map length from real distance, you must DIVIDE real distance by the scale factor.

mistakes.w: Dividing map distance by scale factor to find real length
mistakes.r: To find real distance from map measurement, you must MULTIPLY map distance by scale factor.

mistakes.w: Thinking 1 km = 100 m when converting units
mistakes.r: 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. Remember metric conversions carefully.

mistakes.w: Changing angles when applying a scale factor to a shape
mistakes.r: Angles NEVER change when a shape is scaled or enlarged; only side lengths change.

mistakes.w: Measuring lines from the physical edge of ruler instead of 0 mark
mistakes.r: Always align 0 mark on ruler with the starting point to ensure accurate measurement.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write units in final answer when requested (e.g. 15 instead of 15 km)
mistakes.r: Always include the correct units (m, km, cm) as required by the question prompt.

mistakes.w: Writing a scale ratio as 500 : 1 instead of 1 : 500 for a reduction
mistakes.r: Scale ratios are expressed as Map : Real. For a reduction map, this is always 1 : n.

exam.q: A map has a scale of 1 cm to 4 km. The distance between two villages on the map is 7 cm. Work out the actual distance in kilometres.
model: Real distance = map distance x scale factor
exam.tip: Multiply map distance in cm by the kilometres represented by 1 cm.

exam.q: The scale of a building plan is 1 : 200. The actual length of a room is 12 metres. Calculate the length of this room on the building plan in centimetres.
model: Convert real distance to cm: 12 m = 1200 cm
exam.tip: Convert metres to centimetres first so units match the scale ratio.

exam.q: A scale drawing uses 1 cm to represent 50 metres. Write this scale as a ratio in its simplest form 1 : n.
model: Convert 50 m to cm: 50 x 100 = 5000 cm
exam.tip: Both parts of ratio 1 : n must be in centimetres before removing unit labels.

exam.q: On a map, a road measures 8.5 cm long. The scale of the map is 1 : 25 000. Work out the real length of the road in kilometres.
model: Calculate length in cm: 8.5 x 25 000 = 212 500 cm
exam.tip: Break unit conversion into two clear steps: cm to m, then m to km.

exam.q: A model train is built to a scale of 1 : 87. The model locomotive is 20 cm long. Work out the actual length of the real locomotive in metres.
model: Actual length in cm = 20 x 87 = 1740 cm
exam.tip: Multiply by 87 to find real length in cm, then divide by 100 to give metres.

exam.q: A rectangle has sides of 3 cm and 5 cm. It is enlarged by linear scale factor 4. State the dimensions of the enlarged rectangle and calculate its new perimeter.
exam.tip: Multiply each side length individually by the scale factor 4 before summing for perimeter.

exam.q: The actual distance between two towers is 3.6 km. On a town map, this distance is represented by 12 cm. Find the scale of the map, giving your answer in the form 1 : n.
model: Convert 3.6 km to metres: 3.6 x 1000 = 3600 m
Convert 3600 m to cm: 3600 x 100 = 360 000 cm
exam.tip: Divide real cm distance by map cm distance to calculate n.

exam.q: Town A and Town B are 15 km apart. A map has scale 1 cm to 2.5 km. Point A is marked on the map. Describe how to mark Town B if it lies on a bearing of 060° from Town A.
model: Measure bearing angle clockwise 060° from North line at A
Draw line 6 cm long along 060° direction
Mark point B at end of line
exam.tip: State both the calculated length in cm and the clockwise angle from North.

exam.q: A rectangular garden has real length 18 m and real width 12 m. Draw a scale plan of the garden on a grid where scale is 1 square = 2 metres.
model: Draw rectangle measuring 9 squares by 6 squares on grid
exam.tip: Divide real measurements by grid scale value to determine square counts.

worked.q: A walker plans a route using an Ordnance Survey map with scale 1 : 25 000. On the map, the route measures 16.4 cm. Calculate the real distance of the walk in kilometres.
steps: Step 1: Multiply map distance by scale factor to find real distance in cm.
Step 2: Convert centimetres to metres by dividing by 100.
Step 3: Convert metres to kilometres by dividing by 1000.

worked.q: An architect draws a house floor plan using scale 1 : 50. The real living room is 6.5 metres long and 4.2 metres wide. Calculate the dimensions of the living room on the floor plan in centimetres.
steps: Step 1: Convert real measurements from metres to centimetres.
Length: 6.5 m x 100 = 650 cm
Width: 4.2 m x 100 = 420 cm
Step 2: Divide each centimetre dimension by the scale ratio factor (50).
Drawing length: 650 cm ÷ 50 = 13 cm
Drawing width: 420 cm ÷ 50 = 8.4 cm

worked.q: A scale statement says '2 cm represents 5 km'. Convert this scale statement into a ratio in the form 1 : n.
steps: Step 1: Determine what 1 cm represents by dividing both sides by 2.
1 cm represents 2.5 km
Step 2: Convert 2.5 km into centimetres.
Step 3: Express as unitless ratio 1 : n.

maths_aqa_f.2.3.summary: Ratio notation is a mathematical method used to compare two or more quantities of the same type by showing their relative sizes. A ratio written in the form a : b compares part-to-part, where the order of numbers is strictly tied to the context. Simplest form means reducing a ratio so that all terms are integers with no common factors other than 1, achieved by dividing all terms by their Highest Common Factor (HCF) and ensuring all quantities are in identical units.

core.p: Ratio notation compares quantities using a colon (:) symbol, read aloud as 'to'. It represents how much of one quantity there is compared to another quantity.
bullets: A ratio written as **a : b** compares a quantity **a** to a quantity **b**.
Ratios are **part-to-part** comparisons, whereas fractions usually represent **part-to-whole** relationships.
The colon symbol replacement: '3 red counters to 5 blue counters' is written as **3 : 5**.
Ratios do not show actual amounts; they express the **relative proportional relationship** between quantities.

callouts.p: A mathematical statement comparing two or more quantities by division, showing how many times one value contains another.
In a ratio of red to blue sweets as 2 : 7, 2 parts are red and 7 parts are blue. The total number of parts is 2 + 7 = 9 parts.

core.p: The sequence of numbers in a ratio must strictly mirror the order of the word description in the problem. Reversing the numbers completely changes the context and meaning.
bullets: If a question asks for **cats to dogs**, the number of cats must come **first**.
If there are 4 cats and 9 dogs, the ratio of cats to dogs is **4 : 9**.
Writing **9 : 4** for 'cats to dogs' would incorrectly state there are 9 cats for every 4 dogs.
Always label your ratios with letters above the numbers during working (e.g. C : D) to prevent order errors.

callouts.p: AQA examiners report that reversing ratio terms is one of the most frequent errors on Foundation papers. Always double-check which quantity is named first!

core.p: Equivalent ratios represent the exact same proportional relationship between quantities, even though the numbers used in the ratio look different.
bullets: You obtain an equivalent ratio by **multiplying** or **dividing** every part of the ratio by the **same non-zero number**.
Multiplying both sides scales the ratio up (e.g. 2 : 3 is equivalent to 4 : 6 or 20 : 30).
Dividing both sides scales the ratio down (e.g. 10 : 15 is equivalent to 2 : 3).
Adding or subtracting the same number to/from both parts does **NOT** create an equivalent ratio.

callouts.p: Whatever operation (multiplication or division) you do to one side of a ratio, you MUST do to all other parts.

core.p: A ratio is in its simplest form when all of its terms are whole numbers (integers) that share no common factors other than 1.
bullets: To simplify a ratio, divide all numbers in the ratio by their **Highest Common Factor (HCF)**.
If you do not spot the HCF immediately, you can simplify in **multiple smaller steps** by dividing by smaller common factors (e.g. divide by 2, then by 3).
A ratio in simplest form must consist entirely of **positive whole numbers** (unless specifically requested in the form 1 : n).
Example: To simplify **24 : 36**, find HCF(24, 36) = 12. Divide both terms by 12 to get **2 : 3**.

callouts.p: A ratio expressed using the smallest possible positive whole numbers such that the terms are coprime (their HCF is 1).
If faced with large numbers like 120 : 160, drop the trailing zeros first by dividing by 10 (12 : 16), then divide by 4 to reach 3 : 4.

core.p: Before a ratio containing physical quantities can be simplified, all quantities MUST be converted into the same units of measurement.
bullets: A ratio compare pure numbers; **units must never appear in the final simplified ratio**.
Always convert the larger unit to the smaller unit to avoid introducing decimals during working.
Common unit conversions required in Foundation papers: **£1 = 100p**, **1 kg = 1000g**, **1 m = 100 cm**, **1 cm = 10 mm**, **1 hour = 60 mins**.
Example: Express **40p to £2** as a ratio in simplest form.
Step 1: Convert £2 to pence $\rightarrow$ £2 = 200p.
Step 2: Write ratio without units $\rightarrow$ 40 : 200.
Step 3: Divide both sides by 40 $\rightarrow$ **1 : 5**.

callouts.t: Do Not Keep Units in Ratios
callouts.p: Never write '1p : 5p' or '1cm : 3cm' as your answer. Ratios are unitless numbers.

core.p: Standard ratio form requires integer values. When a ratio contains decimals, eliminate the decimals first before simplifying.
bullets: Multiply all terms by a power of 10 (10, 100, 1000) to clear any decimal places.
If the ratio has 1 decimal place (e.g. 1.5 : 2.5), multiply both terms by **10** $\rightarrow$ 15 : 25.
If one term has 2 decimal places (e.g. 0.8 : 1.25), multiply both terms by **100** $\rightarrow$ 80 : 125.
Once converted to whole numbers, simplify by finding the HCF as normal.

callouts.p: Always check which term has the MOST decimal places. Multiply all terms by 10 if max 1 decimal place, by 100 if max 2 decimal places.

core.p: Ratios containing fractions can be simplified to integer ratios by clearing the denominators.
bullets: Find a **common denominator** for all fractions in the ratio.
Multiply every term in the ratio by this common denominator to eliminate fractions.
Alternatively, cross-multiply for two-term fractional ratios: $\frac{a}{b} : \frac{c}{d} \rightarrow (a \times d) : (b \times c)$.
Example: Simplify **1/4 : 3/8**.
Multiply both terms by 8 $\rightarrow$ $(1/4 \times 8) : (3/8 \times 8) = 2 : 3$.

callouts.p: Never leave fractions inside a final ratio answer unless specifically instructed to write in the form 1 : n.

core.p: Ratios can compare three or more quantities simultaneously. The rules for simplification apply equally across all parts.
bullets: A ratio with three terms takes the form **a : b : c**.
To simplify a three-part ratio, you must divide **all three numbers** by a common factor shared by **all three**.
If a factor divides two of the numbers but not the third, you **cannot** use it.
Example: Simplify **8 : 12 : 20**.
Factors of 8, 12, 20 are shared. HCF(8, 12, 20) = 4.
Divide all three terms by 4 $\rightarrow$ **2 : 3 : 5**.

callouts.p: Do not simplify two parts and leave the third untouched! In 6 : 9 : 10, even though 3 divides 6 and 9, 3 does not divide 10. Thus 6 : 9 : 10 cannot be simplified using 3.

core.h: 9. Expressing Ratios in the Form 1 : n or n : 1 (Unit Ratios)
core.p: In some exam questions, AQA requires ratios to be expressed in the form 1 : n or n : 1. In this form, n does not need to be a whole number; it can be a decimal or fraction.
bullets: To put a ratio in the form **1 : n**, divide both sides of the ratio by the **first number**.
To put a ratio in the form **n : 1**, divide both sides of the ratio by the **second number**.
Example 1: Express **4 : 10** in the form **1 : n**.
Divide both numbers by 4 $\rightarrow$ $4/4 : 10/4 = 1 : 2.5$.
Example 2: Express **5 : 2** in the form **n : 1**.
Divide both numbers by 2 $\rightarrow$ $5/2 : 2/2 = 2.5 : 1$.

callouts.p: Unlike standard ratio simplification, the form 1 : n permits n to be a decimal or fraction because the primary goal is making one side equal to 1.

core.p: To verify that a ratio is fully simplified, check that the resulting numbers are coprime.
bullets: Two integers are **coprime** if their Highest Common Factor is 1.
For example, in the ratio **4 : 9**, even though neither 4 nor 9 are prime numbers, their only common factor is 1, so **4 : 9 is in simplest form**.
Always double-check your answer: can any prime number (2, 3, 5, 7, 11...) divide into all parts?

callouts.p: If one of the numbers in your simplified ratio is 1 or a prime number (and doesn't divide the other numbers), the ratio is guaranteed to be in simplest form!

core.h: 11. Difference Between Ratio and Fraction Notation
core.p: Students frequently confuse ratios with fractions. Understanding the difference between part-to-part and part-to-whole is vital for GCSE exam success.
bullets: Ratio **a : b** compares part **a** to part **b**.
The total number of parts is **a + b**.
The fraction of the whole represented by part **a** is **a / (a + b)**.
The fraction of the whole represented by part **b** is **b / (a + b)**.
Example: In a box with ratio of red to blue bricks = **3 : 5**:
Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8 parts.
Fraction of red bricks = **3/8**.
Fraction of blue bricks = **5/8**.

callouts.p: If the ratio of boys to girls is 2 : 3, the fraction of boys is 2/5 NOT 2/3! Remember to add the ratio parts together to get the denominator.

core.h: 12. Exam Strategies for Ratio Simplification Questions
core.p: AQA GCSE Foundation papers feature ratio notation questions worth between 1 and 3 marks. Follow a disciplined system to guarantee full marks.
bullets: **Read labels carefully**: Identify which item comes first in the wording.
**Unify units**: Convert all amounts to the same unit before writing the ratio numbers.
**Check instruction format**: Look out for 'simplest form' vs 'in the form 1 : n'.
**Show all division steps**: Writing down your common factor division working earns method marks even if a calculation arithmetic error occurs at the end.

callouts.p: 1. Correct order? 2. No units in final answer? 3. Whole numbers (unless 1:n format)? 4. HCF used for simplest form?

analogy.p: Think of ratio notation like a drink mixture recipe that calls for 1 part squash syrup to 4 parts water (1 : 4). Whether you make a small glass (25 ml : 100 ml) or a huge jug (200 ml : 800 ml), the drink tastes exactly the same because the proportional relationship is identical. Simplest form is simply reading the original core recipe (1 : 4) rather than listing the specific volume measurements used in a particular glass. The analogy breaks down because in real recipes, mixing liquids changes total volume dynamically through displacement or dissolving, whereas in mathematical ratio notation, part amounts add up exactly arithmetically.

terms.d: A mathematical comparison of two or more quantities showing their relative sizes.
The format of writing numbers separated by colons (e.g. a : b) to express proportional relationships.
A ratio written using the smallest possible whole numbers where the only common factor is 1.
The largest integer that divides without remainder into two or more given numbers.
Ratios that express the same relative relationship, formed by multiplying or dividing all terms by the same non-zero number.
A ratio expressed in the form 1 : n or n : 1 where one of the terms is equal to 1.
A ratio comparing one component share directly to another component share of a total.
A comparison of one component share relative to the combined total of all shares, usually written as a fraction.
A pair or set of numbers that have no common integer factors other than 1.
An individual number within a ratio.
A ratio of the form a : b : c comparing three distinct quantities concurrently.
The multiplier or divisor used to convert one ratio into an equivalent ratio.

mistakes.w: Writing 15 : 10 as the ratio of apples (10) to oranges (15).
mistakes.r: Writing 10 : 15 (which simplifies to 2 : 3). The order in the ratio must strictly match the word order requested in the question.

mistakes.w: Simplifying 50p to £3 as 50 : 3.
mistakes.r: Converting £3 to 300p first, giving 50 : 300, which simplifies to 1 : 6. Units must be equalized before removing them.

mistakes.w: Leaving units in the final answer, e.g. writing '2cm : 5cm'.
mistakes.r: Writing '2 : 5'. Ratio answers must be pure unitless numbers.

mistakes.w: Leaving a simplified ratio as decimals, e.g. 1.5 : 2.5 when simplest form is requested.
mistakes.r: Multiplying by 2 to get integer values 3 : 5. Standard simplest form requires whole numbers.

mistakes.w: Simplifying 8 : 12 : 15 to 2 : 3 : 15 by dividing only the first two terms by 4.
mistakes.r: Leaving 8 : 12 : 15 as it is because 8, 12, and 15 share no single common factor greater than 1 across ALL three terms.

mistakes.w: Writing 4 : 10 in the form 1 : n as 1 : 2.5 but rounding n to 3.
mistakes.r: Writing 1 : 2.5. In 1 : n form, exact decimals must be preserved unless an explicit rounding instruction is given.

mistakes.w: Thinking the fraction of boys in a 2 : 3 boy to girl ratio is 2/3.
mistakes.r: Calculating total parts (2 + 3 = 5), so the fraction of boys is 2/5.

mistakes.w: Simplifying 12 : 18 by dividing by 2 to get 6 : 9 and stopping there.
mistakes.r: Dividing further by 3 to reach 2 : 3. Simplest form requires reducing until no common factors remain.

exam.q: There are 12 red pens and 20 blue pens in a box. Write the ratio of red pens to blue pens in its simplest form.
model: Write initial ratio in correct order: 12 : 20
Identify HCF of 12 and 20 is 4; divide both terms by 4 to get 3 : 5
exam.tip: Always check that your numbers cannot be divided any further. Both 3 and 5 are prime, so 3 : 5 is fully simplified.

exam.q: Write the ratio 450 g to 1.5 kg in its simplest form.
model: Convert 1.5 kg to grams: 1.5 x 1000 = 1500 g
Divide both sides by HCF 150 (or in steps: divide by 10 to get 45 : 150, then by 15) to get 3 : 10
exam.tip: Never simplify before converting to the same units! 1.5 kg must become 1500 g first.

exam.q: Express the ratio 8 : 28 in the form 1 : n.
model: To get 1 on the left, divide both terms by 8
exam.tip: In '1 : n' form, n can be a decimal. Do not round 3.5 to 4.

exam.q: In a school club, there are 15 boys, 25 girls, and 10 teachers. Write the ratio of boys to girls to teachers in its simplest form.
model: Write three-part ratio in correct order: 15 : 25 : 10
Divide all three terms by common factor 5: (15 / 5) : (25 / 5) : (10 / 5) = 3 : 5 : 2
exam.tip: Make sure you divide ALL three numbers by the same factor.

exam.q: A map scale ratio is written as 2 cm to 5 km. Express this ratio in its simplest form.
model: Convert 5 km to metres: 5 km = 5000 m
Convert 5000 m to centimetres: 5000 x 100 = 500,000 cm
exam.tip: Convert through steps (km -> m -> cm) to avoid missing zeros.

exam.q: Write the ratio 1.2 : 3.6 in its simplest form.
model: Multiply both terms by 10 to clear decimals: 12 : 36
exam.tip: Multiply by 10 first to make both numbers integers before simplifying.

exam.q: A recipe uses 3/4 cup of sugar for every 1.5 cups of flour. Write the ratio of sugar to flour as a ratio of whole numbers in its simplest form.
model: Multiply by 4 to clear fractions/decimals: (0.75 x 4) : (1.5 x 4) = 3 : 6
exam.tip: Converting fractions to decimals or finding a common denominator makes integer conversion straightforward.

exam.q: In a fruit bowl, the ratio of apples to bananas is 3 : 5. What fraction of the fruit in the bowl are apples?
exam.tip: Ratio is part-to-part, fraction is part-to-whole. Add the ratio numbers together for the denominator.

exam.q: Express the ratio 40 : 16 in the form n : 1.
model: To get 1 on the right, divide both terms by 16
exam.tip: Notice the target form is n : 1, so divide by the second number, not the first.

worked.q: A drink is made by mixing 350 ml of fruit juice with 1.4 litres of water. Write the ratio of fruit juice to water in its simplest form.
steps: Step 1: Check units. Juice is in ml (350 ml), water is in litres (1.4 l).
Step 2: Convert litres to ml. 1.4 litres = 1.4 x 1000 = 1400 ml.
Step 3: Write the unsimplified ratio Juice : Water = 350 : 1400.
Step 4: Simplify by dividing both terms by 10 -> 35 : 140.

Step 6: Simplify further by dividing by 5 -> 1 : 4.

maths_aqa_f.2.8.summary: Mastering percentages under AQA GCSE Foundation involves calculating percentage change, finding original values using reverse percentages with multipliers, and computing simple interest for financial maths. You must learn how to convert percentages to decimal multipliers for efficient calculator methods and avoid common traps such as adding and subtracting the wrong base numbers. These financial maths and percentage skills form essential foundations for everyday money management, consumer arithmetic, and higher-tier growth topics.

core.p: A **percentage multiplier** is a single decimal number used to increase or decrease a quantity by a given percentage in one step. Converting a percentage to a decimal is achieved by dividing it by 100. For an increase, add the percentage to 100% before converting; for a decrease, subtract the percentage from 100%.
bullets: To increase an amount by 12%, calculate 100% + 12% = 112%, giving a multiplier of 1.12.
To decrease an amount by 15%, calculate 100% - 15% = 85%, giving a multiplier of 0.85.
Always use decimal multipliers on non-calculator or calculator papers to save time and reduce arithmetic errors.

callouts.p: An increase multiplier is always greater than 1. A decrease multiplier is always less than 1.
Do not use 0.12 as the multiplier for a 12% increase; 0.12 calculates just 12% of the number, not the original plus 12%.

fig.cap: Visual breakdown of a percentage increase multiplier of 1.24 representing 100% plus 24%.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="30" width="360" height="180" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" rx="10"/><rect x="40" y="60" width="240" height="60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="160" y="95" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">100% Original Amount (Multiplier 1.0)</text><rect x="290" y="60" width="80" height="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="95" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">+24%</text><text x="200" y="160" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Total Multiplier = 1.24</text></svg>

core.p: Percentage change measures how much a value has increased or decreased relative to its starting value. The formula must always divide the actual difference by the original value, never the new value.
bullets: Step 1: Find the difference between the new value and the original value (New minus Original).
Step 2: Divide the difference by the original value.
Step 3: Multiply the result by 100 to convert it into a percentage.

callouts.p: Percentage Change = (Actual Difference / Original Value) x 100
Never divide by the new value. The denominator in a percentage change calculation is always the original starting value.

core.p: Reverse percentage problems give you the new value after a percentage increase or decrease, and ask you to find what the value was before. You must use an equation with a multiplier rather than simply adding or subtracting the percentage from the new value.
bullets: Form an equation: Original Value x Multiplier = New Value.
Rearrange the equation: Original Value = New Value / Multiplier.
Calculate the final answer carefully, checking that your original value makes logical sense in context.

callouts.p: Once you find the original value, apply the original percentage increase or decrease to it. If you get the new value given in the question, your answer is correct.
If a jacket costs £44 after a 10% reduction, DO NOT find 10% of 44 and add it back. The 10% was taken from the original price, not the sale price.

core.p: Simple interest is a method of calculating interest where the amount of interest earned each year is a fixed percentage of the original principal amount. The interest does not compound, meaning you earn the exact same amount of money in every time period.
bullets: Formula for annual simple interest: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time.
Principal is the initial amount of money invested or borrowed.
Rate is the annual percentage expressed as a decimal or fraction.
Time is the duration in years.

callouts.p: I = P x r x t, where P is principal, r is decimal interest rate, and t is time in years.
Simple interest represents linear growth because the total amount grows by the same absolute cash value every single year.

core.p: Financial calculations frequently appear in GCSE papers involving earnings, overtime rates, and tax thresholds. You must be able to convert between annual salaries, monthly payments, and weekly or hourly wages.
bullets: There are 52 weeks in a standard year and 12 months in a year.
Overtime is often paid at an enhanced rate, such as 'time and a half' (1.5 times the standard hourly rate) or 'double time' (2 times the standard rate).
Always show clear steps when breaking down annual salaries into weekly or monthly figures.

callouts.p: Memorise that annual salary divided by 12 gives monthly pay, and annual salary divided by 52 gives weekly pay.

core.p: VAT is a government consumption tax placed on most goods and services in the UK. The standard rate of VAT is currently 20%. Exam questions will explicitly state the VAT percentage if it differs from the standard rate.
bullets: To find the total price including VAT, increase the net price by the VAT percentage (usually multiplying by 1.20).
To find the net price (excluding VAT) from the gross price, divide the gross price by the VAT multiplier (usually dividing by 1.20).
Never subtract 20% from a gross price to find the net price.

callouts.p: Finding 20% of the gross price and subtracting it is incorrect because 20% of the larger gross amount is a larger deduction than the original VAT added.

core.h: Financial Mathematics: Best Buys and Unit Pricing
core.p: Consumer arithmetic requires comparing value for money between different pack sizes or offers. To compare items fairly, calculate the unit price (cost per single gram, millilitre, or item) for each option.
bullets: Divide the total cost by the quantity to find the cost per unit.
Compare the unit prices: the lowest cost per unit represents the best value for money.
Ensure both quantities are in the same units (e.g., convert all weights to grams or all volumes to millilitres) before calculating.

callouts.p: Always state your unit price clearly (e.g., pence per 100g) when answering best buy questions to secure method marks.

core.p: Percentage profit and loss calculations compare the financial gain or loss of a business transaction to the original cost price. They follow the exact same structural logic as percentage change.
bullets: Profit = Selling Price - Cost Price (when Selling Price is greater).
Loss = Cost Price - Selling Price (when Cost Price is greater).
Percentage Profit = (Profit / Cost Price) x 100.

callouts.p: Percentage Profit = (Profit / Original Cost Price) x 100
Always divide profit by the original cost price, never by the final selling price.

core.p: Shop sales offer percentage discounts off original prices. You must be comfortable calculating both the monetary savings and the final sale price.
bullets: Method A: Calculate the discount amount by finding the percentage of the original price, then subtract it.
Method B: Multiply the original price by the decrease multiplier to find the sale price directly.
Read the question carefully to check whether it asks for the saving amount or the final discounted price.

callouts.p: Using the multiplier method is faster and less prone to rounding errors in multi-step calculator papers.

core.p: Higher-mark Foundation questions combine multiple percentage operations, such as an increase followed by a decrease, or combining simple interest with annual salary adjustments.
bullets: Break the problem down chronologically into separate steps.
Calculate the outcome of the first percentage operation before applying the second.
Never add percentages together across different bases (e.g., a 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease does not return the original value).

callouts.p: A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease is not a 0% change. Apply each multiplier sequentially.

analogy.t: The Elastic Band Analogy for Percentages and Multipliers
analogy.p: Think of a percentage multiplier as stretching or shrinking an elastic band from a fixed baseline of 1.0. When you increase by 20%, you stretch the band to 1.2 of its original length. When you do a reverse percentage, you are working backwards from the stretched or shrunk length to find out how long the band was before you touched it. The analogy breaks down because an elastic band has physical material limits and non-linear stretching properties, whereas mathematical multipliers scale values infinitely and predictably.

terms.d: Parts per hundred; a fraction or ratio expressed with a denominator of 100.
A decimal number used to scale a quantity up or down in percentage calculations.
The relative change between an original value and a new value, expressed as a percentage.
The initial starting quantity before any percentage increase or decrease was applied.
Working backwards from a final post-increase or post-decrease value to find the original value.
Interest calculated solely on the initial principal amount invested or borrowed over time.
The initial sum of money lent, invested, or borrowed.
Value Added Tax; a government consumption tax added to the price of goods and services.
The price of an item before VAT or additional taxes are added.
The total price of an item after VAT or taxes have been added.
The cost of a single unit of weight, volume, or count for comparison purposes.
The financial gain when an item is sold for more than its original cost price.
The financial deficit when an item is sold for less than its original cost price.
Hours worked beyond regular contracted hours, often paid at an enhanced hourly rate.

mistakes.w: Adding the percentage directly in reverse percentage (e.g., subtracting 10% from the sale price).
mistakes.r: Always use the reverse multiplier equation: Original = New / Multiplier.

mistakes.w: Using 0.05 as the multiplier for a 5% increase.
mistakes.r: A 5% increase requires a multiplier of 1.05.

mistakes.w: Dividing the change by the new value instead of the original value when calculating percentage change.
mistakes.r: The denominator in percentage change is always the original starting value.

mistakes.w: Subtracting 20% from a gross price to find the net price without VAT.
mistakes.r: Divide the gross price by 1.20 to reverse a 20% VAT increase.

mistakes.w: Assuming simple interest compounds each year.
mistakes.r: Simple interest calculates a fixed cash amount based strictly on the original principal every year.

mistakes.w: Comparing pack prices directly without converting to unit prices or matching quantities.
mistakes.r: Always calculate cost per 100g or cost per single item before comparing best buys.

mistakes.w: Calculating percentage profit by dividing profit by the selling price.
mistakes.r: Percentage profit must be divided by the original cost price.

mistakes.w: Combining sequential percentage changes by adding them together (e.g., +10% then +10% equals +20%).
mistakes.r: Apply percentage multipliers sequentially: Multiply the starting value by the first multiplier, then multiply that result by the second multiplier.

exam.q: Increase £340 by 15%.
exam.tip: Use the decimal multiplier 1.15 directly in your calculator.

exam.q: In a sale, the normal price of a television is reduced by 35%. The sale price is £286. Work out the normal price of the television.
exam.tip: Never add 35% to £286. Always divide by the decrease multiplier.

exam.q: A car's value decreases from £12,000 to £9,300. Calculate the percentage decrease in the car's value.
exam.tip: Ensure your denominator is the original value (£12,000), not the new value.

exam.q: Ali invests £2500 in a savings account that pays 3% per annum simple interest. Work out the total amount in the account after 4 years.
model: Calculate total interest for 4 years: £75 x 4 = £300
exam.tip: Simple interest is the same every year. Do not use compound interest formulas.

exam.q: A plumber charges a basic rate of £24 per hour. For overtime hours, the rate is increased by 50%. How much does the plumber earn for 6 hours of overtime?
model: Multiply by number of overtime hours: £36 x 6
exam.tip: An increase of 50% corresponds to a multiplier of 1.5.

exam.q: The price of a bicycle including VAT at 20% is £360. What is the price of the bicycle before VAT?
exam.tip: Dividing by 1.20 reverses a 20% addition correctly.

exam.q: Shop A sells 400g of cheese for £2.80. Shop B sells 550g of cheese for £3.74. Which shop offers the better value for money? You must show your working.
model: Calculate unit price for Shop A: 280p / 400 = 0.7p per gram (or £0.007 per g)
Calculate unit price for Shop B: 374p / 550 = 0.68p per gram
Conclusion: Shop B offers better value
exam.tip: Find the cost per 1g or cost per 100g for both items to compare.

exam.q: A shopkeeper buys a rug for £80 and sells it for £104. Calculate her percentage profit.
exam.tip: Always divide profit by the cost price (£80), not the selling price.

exam.q: Imran's salary is £28,000. He receives a pay rise of 4%. What is his new salary?
exam.tip: Using 1.04 gives the new total in one single calculation.

exam.q: A house appreciates in value by 10% in Year 1, and then depreciates in value by 10% in Year 2. If the original house price was £200,000, find its value after Year 2.
exam.tip: Apply each percentage change sequentially to the running total.

worked.q: A jacket in a sale has a reduced price of £51 after a 15% discount. Calculate the original price of the jacket before the sale.
steps: Determine the multiplier for a 15% decrease: 100% - 15% = 85%, which gives 0.85.
Set up the reverse percentage equation: Original Price x 0.85 = 51.
Rearrange and calculate: Original Price = 51 / 0.85.
Compute the division to get £60.

worked.q: Sarah invests £4000 in an account paying 4% per annum simple interest. Calculate the total value of her investment after 5 years.
steps: Calculate the annual simple interest earned: £4000 x 0.04 = £160 per year.
Multiply the annual interest by the number of years: £160 x 5 = £800 total interest.
Add the total interest to the original principal: £4000 + £800 = £4800.

maths_aqa_f.2.7.summary: This comprehensive revision guide explores how to seamlessly bridge the gap between ratios, fractions, and linear functions. You will master converting parts of a ratio into fractional shares of a whole, as well as expressing linear relationships algebraically using proportional equations. Understanding these connections is essential for solving complex multi-step Foundation tier problems in AQA GCSE Mathematics.

core.p: A ratio compares parts of a whole to one another, whereas a fraction compares a part to the entire whole. Translating between these two representations allows you to find exact quantities when given only a total amount or a fractional part.
bullets: Given the ratio a : b, the total number of parts is a + b.
The fraction representing the first part (a) is a / (a + b).
The fraction representing the second part (b) is b / (a + b).
The sum of all fractional parts in a ratio must always equal exactly 1.

callouts.p: To convert part of a ratio to a fraction, place that part's value as the numerator and the sum of all parts in the ratio as the denominator.
Always add the numbers in the ratio together to find your denominator. Forgetting to add them and using just one number is a very common exam error.

fig.cap: Visualising the ratio 3:2 as fractions out of a total of 5 equal parts.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="40" width="360" height="160" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="40" y="80" width="210" height="60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="250" y="80" width="140" height="60" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="145" y="115" font-size="14" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">3 parts (3/5)</text><text x="320" y="115" font-size="14" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">2 parts (2/5)</text><text x="200" y="65" font-size="14" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Total = 5 parts (Whole = 1)</text></svg>

core.p: Sometimes an exam question gives you information in the form of fractions and asks you to state a ratio. You can reverse the conversion process by taking the numerators of fractions that share a common denominator.
bullets: If part A is 2/7 of a total and part B is 5/7 of the total, the ratio is 2 : 5.
Ensure both fractions share the same denominator before extracting the ratio parts.
Simplify the resulting ratio fully by dividing by any common factors.
Check that your ratio parts add up to give the correct proportional total.

callouts.p: Fractions must have the same denominator to directly read off their numerators as a ratio of parts to parts.

core.h: 3. Using Fractions to Find Quantities from Ratios
core.p: When dividing an actual physical quantity (like money, weight, or length) using a given ratio, converting the ratio to fractions is often the quickest and most robust method.
bullets: Calculate the total number of parts in the given ratio.
Express each person's or item's share as a fraction of the total.
Multiply the total quantity by the fraction to find the exact value.
Verify your final answers by adding them back together to match the original total.

callouts.p: Multiplying a total amount by a fraction (e.g., 3/8 * 40) is equivalent to dividing by the denominator and multiplying by the numerator.

core.h: 4. Introduction to Linear Functions in Ratio Contexts
core.p: A linear function describes a straight-line relationship between two variables, typically written in the form y = mx + c. In ratio problems, a fixed ratio between two variables creates a direct linear relationship where the line passes through the origin (c = 0).
bullets: Direct proportionality means y = mx, where m is the constant ratio or multiplier.
The ratio of y to x is always constant: y / x = m.
On a graph, this is represented by a straight line passing through (0, 0).
The gradient (m) of the line represents the ratio value.

callouts.p: A linear function linking two quantities in a fixed ratio takes the algebraic form y = kx, where k is the constant ratio.

fig.cap: A linear graph representing a direct ratio y = 2x passing through the origin.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="20" width="360" height="200" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="40" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="300" y2="60" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="340" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">x</text><text x="40" y="50" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">y</text><text x="60" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">0</text><text x="180" y="140" font-size="12" fill="#2563eb" text-anchor="middle">y = 2x</text></svg>

core.p: Ratio statements can be translated directly into algebraic equations. For instance, if the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 4, we can write the number of boys as 3x and the number of girls as 4x.
bullets: Replace ratio parts with algebraic expressions using a common multiplier x.
Equate the sum of the algebraic parts to the given total if applicable.
Solve the resulting linear equation to find the value of x.
Substitute x back into the expressions to find individual quantities.

callouts.p: Do not confuse the ratio numbers with the actual amounts. Always introduce an unknown variable multiplier like x.

core.h: 6. Writing Linear Equations from Proportional Statements
core.p: When two quantities are in a constant ratio, any change in one results in a predictable linear change in the other. This forms the basis of scaling recipes, currency conversion, and best-buy problems.
bullets: Identify the independent variable (input, x) and dependent variable (output, y).
Determine the scale factor or unit rate linking them.
Construct the linear equation in the format y = mx.
Use the equation to calculate missing values for any given input.

callouts.p: The multiplier m in y = mx is known as the constant of proportionality and represents the ratio value.

core.p: To determine which of two ratios is larger, or to compare different mixtures, convert each ratio into a fraction with a common denominator or convert them into decimals/percentages.
bullets: Express each ratio as a fraction of its total.
Find a common denominator for the fractions to allow direct comparison.
Compare the numerators to see which ratio represents a greater proportion.
Alternatively, convert the fractions into decimals by dividing numerator by denominator.

callouts.p: Converting ratio fractions to decimals makes comparing proportions across different total sizes much faster in calculator papers.

core.h: 8. Graphical Representation of Linear Functions in Ratio
core.p: Linear functions derived from ratios can be plotted on Cartesian axes. The steepness of the line corresponds directly to the ratio value, providing a visual way to read off proportional values.
bullets: Create a table of values using the linear ratio equation y = mx.
Plot coordinate pairs (x, y) accurately on the grid.
Draw a straight line through the points and extend it through the origin (0, 0).
Use the line to read intermediate values that are not whole numbers.

callouts.p: A linear function representing direct ratio must always pass through the coordinate origin (0, 0) because zero input gives zero output.

core.h: 9. Solving Word Problems Involving Ratios and Fractions
core.p: Exam questions often combine ratio statements with fractional parts of quantities. Breaking the problem down into manageable linear statements is the key to full marks.
bullets: Translate sentences into mathematical ratios or fractions step by step.
Assign variables clearly (e.g., let total amount be T).
Set up an equation linking the fraction of the total to a given numerical value.
Solve the linear equation and check units in your final answer.

callouts.p: Always write down what your variable represents at the start of your working out (e.g., 'Let x be the number of red counters').

core.p: While direct proportion links ratios via y = mx, indirect or inverse proportion describes situations where as one variable increases, the other decreases at a proportional rate.
bullets: Inverse proportion is represented algebraically as xy = k or y = k / x.
The product of the two quantities remains constant.
On a graph, an inverse proportion produces a curve called a hyperbola, not a straight line.
Foundation tier students must recognise the algebraic form y = k / x.

callouts.p: Do not draw a straight line for inverse proportion; inverse proportion produces a curved graph.

core.h: 11. Exam Technique for Ratio and Linear Function Questions
core.p: Examiners award method marks even if calculation errors occur. Setting out your conversion from ratio to fractions clearly is vital for securing partial credit.
bullets: Show every step of your fraction conversion clearly.
State the total number of parts explicitly before calculating fractional shares.
Check if your final answer answers the specific question asked.
Ensure ratios are fully simplified and fractions are in their lowest terms.

callouts.p: Writing down the total number of parts (e.g., 3 + 4 = 7) often secures a method mark even if the final arithmetic goes wrong.

analogy.p: Imagine making a fruit smoothie using a ratio of 2 parts strawberries to 3 parts banana. The total number of parts in your blender is 5. Therefore, strawberries make up exactly 2/5 of the entire smoothie, and banana makes up 3/5. If you decide to make a bigger batch, you multiply both fruit amounts by the same linear scale factor x, giving the linear function y = (2/3)x for the relationship between the two fruits. This breaks down when ingredients react chemically and do not just add up linearly, but for GCSE maths, quantities always scale perfectly.

terms.d: A comparison of two or more quantities showing the relative sizes of the parts.
A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, representing a part of a whole.
A function that graphs as a straight line, typically written in the form y = mx + c.
The constant multiplier (m) linking two variables in direct proportion (y = mx).
A relationship between two quantities where an increase in one leads to a proportional increase in the other.
A relationship where an increase in one variable leads to a proportional decrease in the other.
Reducing a ratio or fraction to its lowest terms by dividing by common factors.
The sum of all individual numbers in a given ratio.
The steepness of a linear graph, calculated as change in y divided by change in x.
The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis intersect on a Cartesian graph.
Corresponding in size or amount to something else.
An equation that uses letters to represent real-world relationships and quantities.

mistakes.w: Writing a ratio as a fraction without adding the parts for the denominator (e.g., ratio 3 : 2 becomes fraction 3/2).
mistakes.r: The denominator must be the total number of parts (3 + 2 = 5), so the fraction is 3/5.

mistakes.w: Adding the ratio numbers together and multiplying them by the wrong quantity.
mistakes.r: Multiply the total amount by the individual fractional share (e.g., 3/5 * total).

mistakes.w: Assuming a linear function representing a ratio can have any y-intercept c other than 0.
mistakes.r: Direct ratio functions always pass through the origin, meaning c = 0 (y = mx).

mistakes.w: Inverting the ratio when converting to fractions (writing 2 : 3 as 3/5 for the first part).
mistakes.r: The first number in the ratio corresponds to the numerator of the first part's fraction.

mistakes.w: Drawing a curved line for a direct proportion or linear function graph.
mistakes.r: Direct proportion and linear functions always form a straight line.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the variable multiplier x when setting up ratio equations.
mistakes.r: Always use 3x, 4x etc., when breaking a ratio into algebraic parts for an equation.

mistakes.w: Comparing ratios by looking only at the first number without considering the total parts.
mistakes.r: Convert ratios into fractions with common denominators before comparing them.

exam.q: Write the ratio 3 : 5 as a fraction representing the first part.
exam.tip: Add 3 and 5 to get the total denominator of 8.

exam.q: In a bag of counters, the ratio of red to blue counters is 4 : 1. What fraction of the counters are blue?
exam.tip: Blue is the second part of the ratio, so it forms the numerator.

exam.q: Share 45 sweets between Anna and Ben in the ratio 2 : 7. Use fractions to find how many sweets Ben gets.
exam.tip: Calculate Ben's fractional share first before multiplying by the total.

exam.q: A linear function is given by the equation y = 4x. State the ratio of y to x in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Rearrange y = 4x to y/x = 4 to see the ratio clearly.

exam.q: The ratio of cats to dogs in a shelter is 3 : 4. There are 28 dogs. Write a linear equation linking cats (c) and dogs (d).
exam.tip: Express one variable in terms of the other using the ratio fraction.

exam.q: Which ratio is greater: 2 : 3 or 3 : 5? Show your working.
model: 2 : 3 is greater because 10/15 is larger than 9/15
exam.tip: Convert both ratios to fractions with a common denominator of 15.

exam.q: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 5 : 2. If x grams of flour are used, write down an expression for the mass of sugar in terms of x.
model: Sugar is 2 parts out of 5 for flour, so sugar = (2 / 5)x
exam.tip: Set up the multiplier based on the ratio of sugar to flour.

exam.q: Sketch a graph of the linear function representing the direct ratio y = 3x, passing through the origin.
exam.tip: Ensure the line goes strictly through the origin (0, 0).

exam.q: In a school, 3/8 of the students are boys and the rest are girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Subtract the numerator from the denominator to find the remaining fraction for girls.

exam.q: Two quantities x and y are in direct proportion. When x = 4, y = 10. Write the linear equation connecting y and x.
exam.tip: Find the constant of proportionality m by doing y divided by x.

worked.q: A man divides £72 between his two children, Sam and Mia, in the ratio 4 : 5. (a) What fraction of the total does Mia receive? (b) How much money does Mia actually get?
steps: Step 1: Find the total number of parts in the ratio. Total parts = 4 + 5 = 9.
Step 2: Write Mia's share as a fraction. Mia corresponds to the second number (5), so her fraction is 5 / 9.
Step 3: Calculate Mia's actual money by multiplying the total amount by her fraction. (£72 / 9) * 5 = 8 * 5 = £40.

worked.q: The ratio of red counters to green counters in a bag is 3 : 5. There are 24 red counters. Write a linear equation connecting the number of red counters (r) and green counters (g), and use it to find the number of green counters.
steps: Step 1: Write the ratio as a proportional fraction statement: r / g = 3 / 5.
Step 2: Rearrange to form a linear function for green counters: g = (5 / 3)r.
Step 3: Substitute r = 24 into the equation: g = (5 / 3) * 24.
Step 4: Calculate the result: g = 5 * 8 = 40 green counters.
worked.ans: g = (5/3)r, and there are 40 green counters.

maths_aqa_f.2.9.summary: Direct and inverse proportion describes mathematical relationships where quantities increase or decrease together at a constant rate, or where one variable increases as another decreases by multiplying to a constant. Mastery of these concepts requires setting up algebraic equations using the proportionality constant k, finding k from given values, and interpreting their graphical representations on Cartesian planes. Foundation tier students must accurately distinguish between straight-line direct proportion graphs passing through the origin and curved inverse proportion hyperbola graphs.

core.p: Proportion compares how two quantities relate to one another. When two variables are related such that a change in one produces a consistent, predictable change in the other, we say they are in proportion.
bullets: Direct proportion means as one variable increases, the other increases at the same rate.
Inverse proportion means as one variable increases, the other decreases.
The constant of proportionality is represented by the letter k.
Proportion questions always require finding the value of k first before answering the final question.

callouts.p: A statement that two ratios or rates are equal.
Always write out the general proportional equation with k before substituting any numbers.

core.p: When y is directly proportional to x, it is written algebraically using the proportionality symbol or an equals sign with a constant k.
bullets: Written as y proportional to x, or y equals k multiplied by x.
The constant k is calculated by doing y divided by x.
Doubling x will always double the value of y.
Halving x will always halve the value of y.

callouts.p: y = kx
Never use addition like y = x + k for direct proportion. It must always be multiplication.

core.h: Finding the Constant in Direct Proportion
core.p: To solve direct proportion problems completely, you must find the exact numerical value of k using a complete pair of given values.
bullets: Substitute the given x and y values into the formula y = kx.
Rearrange the equation to isolate k.
Keep k as an exact fraction or decimal for subsequent calculations.
Use your found value of k to answer the final part of the question.

callouts.p: k = y / x is your go-to rearrangement for finding the constant.

core.p: The graph of two directly proportional variables has a very distinct and recognisable visual appearance on a set of axes.
bullets: The graph is always a straight line.
The line must pass through the exact origin (0, 0).
The gradient of the straight line is equal to the constant of proportionality k.
If the line does not pass through (0, 0), the variables are in linear correlation but not direct proportion.

callouts.p: Straight line passing through the origin (0, 0).

fig.cap: A direct proportion graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient k.

core.p: When y is inversely proportional to x, as one variable gets bigger, the other gets smaller at a reciprocal rate.
bullets: Written as y proportional to 1 divided by x.
Formulated algebraically as y equals k divided by x.
Rearranges to give the constant product rule: x multiplied by y equals k.
Doubling x will halve the value of y.

callouts.p: y = k / x or xy = k
Do not write y = k - x for inverse proportion. Inverse involves division or reciprocal.

core.h: Finding the Constant in Inverse Proportion
core.p: Finding the constant for inverse proportion uses multiplication rather than division of the given variable pairs.
bullets: Substitute the given x and y values into the formula xy = k.
Multiply x and y together to find the exact value of k.
Substitute k back into y = k / x to create your working formula.
Use the working formula to calculate missing values.

callouts.p: For inverse proportion, corresponding pairs always multiply to give the exact same constant k.

core.p: The graphical representation of inverse proportion looks very different from direct proportion due to the division relationship.
bullets: The graph forms a curve known as a rectangular hyperbola.
The curve never touches either the x-axis or the y-axis because x and y can never equal zero.
As x values get very large, y values get very close to zero.
As x values get close to zero, y values shoot up towards infinity.

callouts.p: A downward sloping curve that never touches the axes.

fig.cap: An inverse proportion graph is a hyperbola that never touches the axes.
