core.p: Proportion is frequently tested using real-life contexts like recipes, sharing work between people, or currency exchanges.
bullets: If 5 workers take 12 hours to build a wall, more workers will take less time (inverse proportion).
If 3 apples cost 1.50 pounds, 7 apples will cost more (direct proportion).
Always check whether the relationship is direct or inverse before calculating.
Workers and time are classic inverse scenarios because people working faster reduces total time.

callouts.p: Ask yourself: if one quantity goes up, should the other go up (direct) or down (inverse)?

analogy.p: Direct proportion is like buying bags of sweets: buy twice as many bags, and you pay twice as much money. Inverse proportion is like sharing a fixed bag of 24 sweets among friends: the more friends that arrive, the fewer sweets each person receives. Where the analogy breaks down is that people and sweets usually come in whole integer amounts, whereas mathematical proportions work continuously with any decimal or fraction.

terms.d: A relationship between two variables where an increase in one causes a proportional increase in the other, maintain a constant ratio.
A relationship where an increase in one variable results in a proportional decrease in the other, maintaining a constant product.
The constant multiplier, represented by k, that links proportional variables together.
The curved graphical shape produced by inverse proportion equations.
The point (0, 0) on a Cartesian graph where the x-axis and y-axis intersect.
An equation showing that two ratios are equal.
A quantity that can change or take on different numerical values, usually represented by a letter.
The steepness of a graph line, equal to vertical change divided by horizontal change.
One divided by a number or quantity.
Replacing algebraic letters with known numerical values.
A pair of numbers (x, y) that locate a specific point on a grid.
A reference line on a graph used for measurement.

mistakes.w: Writing y = x + k for direct proportion
mistakes.r: Direct proportion must always use multiplication: y = kx.

mistakes.w: Dividing x by y to find k in inverse proportion
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion requires multiplying x and y together: k = xy.

mistakes.w: Assuming a straight line graph not passing through the origin is direct proportion
mistakes.r: The line must pass through (0, 0) to be direct proportion.

mistakes.w: Thinking more workers means more time taken
mistakes.r: More workers mean less time taken, which is inverse proportion.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to find the value of k before answering the final question
mistakes.r: Always calculate k as your first working step.

mistakes.w: Drawing an inverse proportion curve that crosses the axes
mistakes.r: Hyperbolas approach but never touch the axes.

mistakes.w: Using direct proportion methods for inverse proportion word problems
mistakes.r: Carefully read whether variables increase together or oppose each other.

exam.q: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 4, y = 20. Find an equation linking y and x.
exam.tip: State the general formula first before finding k.

exam.q: y is inversely proportional to x. When x = 2, y = 12. Find the value of y when x = 8.
model: xy = k or y = k / x
exam.tip: Multiply x and y to find k for inverse proportion.

exam.q: Explain why the graph of y = 3x + 1 does not show direct proportion.
model: The graph does not pass through the origin (0, 0).
exam.tip: Mention the origin for direct proportion graph questions.

exam.q: 5 machines can complete a factory order in 6 days. Assuming all machines work at the same rate, how many days will 3 machines take?
model: Identify inverse proportion: total machine-days = 5 multiplied by 6 = 30
Divide total work by new number of machines: 30 / 3
exam.tip: Find total workload (machine-days) for inverse proportion context problems.

exam.q: y is directly proportional to x squared. When x = 3, y = 45. Find y when x = 4.
model: 45 = k multiplied by 3 squared (9), so k = 5
exam.tip: Square x before finding k when the question specifies x squared.

exam.q: Sketch a sketch of an inverse proportion graph on axes with positive x and y.
model: Curve sloping downwards from left to right
Curve does not touch x or y axes
exam.tip: Ensure your hyperbola curve stays clear of both axes.

exam.q: y is inversely proportional to x. Complete the table: x = 4, y = ?; x = 8, y = 3.
exam.tip: Use the constant product xy to fill in missing table values.

exam.q: State whether the relationship between the number of petrol litres bought and total cost is direct or inverse.
exam.tip: More petrol costs more money, so it is direct.

exam.q: y is directly proportional to x. If x increases by 50 percent, what is the percentage increase in y?
model: Direct proportion means variables change by the exact same proportion
exam.tip: Direct proportion scales variables by identical multiplicative factors.

worked.q: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 6, y = 21. (a) Find the equation connecting y and x. (b) Find y when x = 14.
steps: Write down the direct proportion formula: y = kx.
Substitute x = 6 and y = 21 into the formula to find k: 21 = 6k.
Solve for k: k = 21 / 6 = 3.5.
Write part (a) equation: y = 3.5x.
Substitute x = 14 into the equation for part (b): y = 3.5 multiplied by 14.
Calculate final answer: y = 49.

worked.q: It takes 4 builders 15 days to build a brick wall. Assuming they work at the same rate, how many days would it take 10 builders?
steps: Recognise that this is inverse proportion because more builders will take fewer days.
Calculate the constant k (total builder-days): 4 multiplied by 15 = 60.
Set up the inverse proportion equation: n multiplied by d = 60, where n is number of builders and d is days.
Substitute n = 10 into the equation: 10 multiplied by d = 60.
Solve for d: d = 60 / 10 = 6.

maths_aqa_f.2.5.summary: This revision module covers expressing a multiplicative relationship between two quantities as a ratio or fraction for the AQA GCSE Foundation tier. It provides clear guidance on translating word statements, scale factors, and practical comparisons into formal mathematical notation. Students will learn the step-by-step processes to simplify ratios, build proper fractions, and navigate common exam pitfalls to secure full marks.

core.p: A multiplicative relationship compares two quantities by showing how many times larger one is than the other, rather than using addition or subtraction. In the Foundation tier, recognizing these links allows us to translate everyday statements into exact mathematical ratios and fractions.
bullets: Compares two quantities using multiplication and division.
Ignores additive differences (e.g., '6 more than') in favour of scale factors ('3 times as many').
Forms the foundational bedrock for ratios, proportions, fractions, and scaling.

callouts.p: A comparison between two numbers or quantities expressed through multiplication or division, showing proportional scaling.
Look out for phrases like 'per', 'for every', 'times as many', and 'ratio of' in exam questions.

core.p: To express a multiplicative link as a ratio, we identify the two distinct quantities and write them in the order specified by the question using the colon notation. Maintaining the correct sequence is vital for avoiding reversed-mark penalties.
bullets: Identify Quantity A and Quantity B from the problem text.
Write them in the exact order requested using the colon symbol (Quantity A : Quantity B).
Ensure both quantities are converted into the exact same units before writing the ratio.

callouts.p: If a question asks for the ratio of boys to girls and there are 12 boys and 18 girls, the answer is 12 : 18, not 18 : 12.

core.p: Just like fractions, ratios should be written in their simplest form by dividing all parts by their highest common factor (HCF). This reveals the fundamental multiplicative relationship in its most reduced state.
bullets: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of all numbers in the ratio.
Divide every number in the ratio by this HCF.
Check that no further common factors remain other than 1.

callouts.p: A ratio is fully simplified when all parts are whole numbers and share no common integer factors.

core.p: Before establishing a ratio or fraction between two quantities, they must be expressed in identical units. Comparing centimetres to metres directly without converting will result in an incorrect mathematical relationship.
bullets: Check units for both quantities before writing any ratio.
Convert the larger unit to the smaller unit using standard metric multipliers (e.g., 1 m = 100 cm).
Never include unit labels (like cm, kg, or £) inside the final ratio notation.

callouts.p: Ratios are dimensionless. Writing 20 cm : 1 m as 20 : 1 is wrong; convert to 20 : 100 first, then simplify to 1 : 5.

core.h: Expressing a Ratio as a Fraction
core.p: Any part-to-part or part-to-whole relationship expressed as a ratio can be translated into a fraction. The total number of parts forms the denominator, while the specific part forms the numerator.
bullets: Sum all the individual parts of a ratio to find the whole denominator (e.g., for 3 : 5, total parts = 3 + 5 = 8).
Place the specific quantity's value over the total to form the fraction.
Simplify the resulting fraction if possible.

callouts.p: If a ratio of red to blue counters is 2 : 3, the fraction of red counters is 2 / (2 + 3) = 2/5.

fig.cap: Visualising ratio parts as fractions using partitioned shapes.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="50" y="40" width="300" height="60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" rx="6"/><line x1="150" y1="40" x2="150" y2="100" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="85" y="75" fill="#1b2540" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Part A (2)</text><text x="200" y="75" fill="#1b2540" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Part B (3)</text><text x="50" y="140" fill="#1b2540" font-size="13">Ratio A : B = 2 : 3</text><text x="50" y="165" fill="#1b2540" font-size="13">Fraction of A = 2 / 5</text><text x="50" y="190" fill="#1b2540" font-size="13">Fraction of B = 3 / 5</text></svg>

core.h: Expressing One Quantity as a Fraction of Another
core.p: When asked to express Quantity A as a fraction of Quantity B, Quantity A becomes the numerator and Quantity B becomes the denominator. This establishes a direct multiplicative fraction comparing the two values.
bullets: Identify the target quantity that goes on top (numerator).
Identify the reference quantity that goes on the bottom (denominator).
Simplify the fraction by dividing numerator and denominator by their HCF.

callouts.p: Whatever follows the word 'of' always goes on the bottom of the fraction.

core.p: A multiplicative relationship can be stated as a scaling factor, indicating how much larger or smaller one quantity is compared to another. Dividing the second quantity by the first yields this exact multiplier.
bullets: Calculate multiplier = Quantity B / Quantity A.
Use the multiplier to scale values up or down directly.
Recognize that multipliers greater than 1 represent growth, while values between 0 and 1 represent reduction.

callouts.p: A number which scales, or multiplies, some quantity.

core.p: Exam questions frequently require students to take mixed real-world data, convert them into a consistent format, and express their multiplicative relationship as a simplified ratio.
bullets: Extract numerical values carefully from wordy problem descriptions.
Ensure consistent units and categories before setting up the comparison.
Reduce the resulting ratio fully and verify your work.

callouts.p: Always check your final ratio numbers for hidden common factors like 2, 3, 5, or 7.

fig.cap: Comparison of fruit quantities expressed as a simplified ratio.

core.p: Moving in reverse, if given a fraction representing part of a whole or part-to-part relationship, we can instantly extract the corresponding ratio notation by reading the numerator and denominator directly.
bullets: A fraction a/b directly corresponds to the ratio a : (b - a) if it is a part-to-part comparison.
A fraction a/b represents part-to-whole as a : b.
Always clarify whether the question refers to part-to-part or part-to-whole.

callouts.t: Watch Out for Part-to-Part vs Part-to-Whole
callouts.p: Do not confuse fractions of a whole with direct ratios between two separate items.

core.h: Multiplicative Relationships in Money and Finance
core.p: Money comparisons often involve different currencies or splitting amounts. Expressing these relationships correctly requires strict attention to pounds and pence, or euros and cents.
bullets: Convert all monetary amounts into pence (£1 = 100p) if dealing with mixed pounds and pence.
Write the ratio of one person's money to another in simplest form.
Express individual shares as fractions of the total pooled amount.

callouts.p: Comparing £2.50 to 75p? Convert £2.50 to 250p first to get 250 : 75.

core.p: Multiplicative relationships can extend beyond two quantities to three or more quantities. Each maintains its proportional share within the combined whole.
bullets: Write three quantities in sequence using colons (A : B : C).
Simplify by dividing all three numbers by their common HCF.
Find individual fractional parts by placing each number over the grand total sum.

callouts.p: For ratio 2 : 3 : 5, the total parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10. Fractions are 2/10, 3/10, and 5/10.

core.p: Securing top marks on multiplicative relationship questions requires systematic working out, clear unit conversions, and verifying that ratios and fractions are fully reduced.
bullets: Always show your unsimplified ratio or fraction before reducing.
Double-check unit conversions (e.g., cm to m, grams to kg).
Ensure your final answer matches the exact format requested by the command words.

callouts.p: Even if your final simplification slips up, examiners award method marks for correct initial unit conversions and setup.

analogy.p: Imagine making orange squash: you mix 1 part cordial with 4 parts water. The multiplicative relationship is fixed at 1 : 4. If you change units or make a larger jug, the ratio remains identical because every single glass follows the exact same multiplicative scaling. Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical or physical mixtures sometimes experience volume contraction or non-linear interactions, whereas mathematical ratios remain perfectly constant.

terms.d: A mathematical comparison of two or more quantities showing their relative sizes.
A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, representing part of a whole or part of another quantity.
A ratio or fraction reduced by dividing all numbers by their highest common factor.
The largest positive integer that divides evenly into two or more numbers.
A multiplier used to scale one quantity up or down relative to another.
Ensuring all quantities in a comparison are measured in the exact same units.
A ratio comparing one subgroup directly to another subgroup within a total.
A comparison showing a specific part relative to the entire combined total.
The top number in a fraction representing the chosen part.
The bottom number in a fraction representing the total parts.
A link between quantities expressed in terms of multiplication and division rather than addition.
An equality between two ratios.

mistakes.w: Writing 50 cm : 2 m as 50 : 2
mistakes.r: Convert units first so they match: 50 cm : 200 cm, which simplifies to 1 : 4.

mistakes.w: Leaving a ratio unsimplified as 12 : 18
mistakes.r: Divide by the HCF (6) to give the required simplest form 2 : 3.

mistakes.w: Including units like 'kg' or 'cm' inside the final ratio notation
mistakes.r: Ratios are dimensionless numbers; never write unit labels inside a ratio.

mistakes.w: Reversing order when asked for ratio of girls to boys
mistakes.r: Read carefully: if girls are first, write girls : boys in that exact order.

mistakes.w: Writing a fraction as part-to-part instead of part-to-whole
mistakes.r: Fractions of a total must have the grand total sum as the denominator.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to check for further common factors after one division step
mistakes.r: Always check if the numbers can be divided again until no common factors remain.

mistakes.w: Treating ratio as an addition problem (e.g., adding instead of multiplying)
mistakes.r: Ratios are multiplicative comparisons; use scaling and division.

exam.q: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours in its simplest form.
model: Convert 2 hours to minutes: 2 x 60 = 120 minutes.
Simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 15 to get 3 / 8.
exam.tip: Always convert to the smaller unit first so both numbers share the same unit.

exam.q: In a class, there are 12 boys and 18 girls. Write the ratio of boys to total students in its simplest form.
model: Simplify by dividing by 6 to give 2 : 5.
exam.tip: Read carefully: this asks for boys to total, not boys to girls.

exam.q: A bag contains red counters and blue counters. The ratio of red to blue counters is 3 : 5. What fraction of the counters are red?
model: Place red parts over total parts: 3 / 8.
exam.tip: Part-to-whole fractions use the sum of all ratio parts as the denominator.

exam.q: Express £1.50 as a ratio of 75p in simplest form.
model: Simplify by dividing by 75 to get 2 : 1.
exam.tip: Convert pounds to pence to avoid decimals in your ratio.

exam.q: There are 24 dogs and 16 cats at a rescue centre. Write the ratio of cats to dogs in its simplest form.
model: Identify order: cats to dogs means 16 : 24.
Find HCF of 16 and 24, which is 8.
exam.tip: Check the requested order: cats first, dogs second.

exam.q: A recipe uses 400g of flour and 160g of butter. Write the ratio of flour to butter in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Canceling trailing zeros is a quick way to start simplifying large numbers.

exam.q: Express 35 cm as a fraction of 2 metres in its simplest form.
model: Simplify by dividing by 5 to get 7 / 40.
exam.tip: Never compare cm and m directly without converting.

exam.q: In a car park, there are 40 red cars, 24 blue cars, and 16 silver cars. Write the ratio of red to blue to silver cars in its simplest form.
model: Find HCF for all three numbers, which is 8.
exam.tip: The HCF must divide evenly into ALL parts of a multi-part ratio.

exam.q: A school has 600 students. 250 are in Key Stage 4 and the rest are in Key Stage 3. Express the ratio of Key Stage 3 students to Key Stage 4 students in its simplest form.
model: Simplify by dividing by 50 to get 7 : 5.
exam.tip: Calculate missing sub-totals first before forming the ratio.

exam.q: A rope of length 4.5 metres is cut into two pieces in the ratio 2 : 7. Express the length of the shorter piece as a fraction of the total rope.
exam.tip: You do not need the actual length of 4.5m to find the fraction of the total.

worked.q: Express 750 grams as a fraction of 3 kilograms in its simplest form.
steps: Convert kilograms to grams: 3 kg = 3000 g.
Write the quantities as a fraction with 750 as the numerator and 3000 as the denominator: 750 / 3000.
Simplify the fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by their HCF (750), resulting in 1 / 4.

worked.q: A football team plays 30 matches. They win 14, draw 6, and lose 10. Express the ratio of wins to draws to losses in its simplest form.
steps: Write the initial ratio in the order requested (Wins : Draws : Losses): 14 : 6 : 10.
Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) for 14, 6, and 10, which is 2.
Divide each part of the ratio by 2 to get the simplified three-part ratio: 7 : 3 : 5.

maths_aqa_f.2.13.summary: Master the concepts of gradient as a rate of change and graphs of direct and inverse proportion for AQA GCSE Foundation. Learn how to calculate gradients from real-life straight-line graphs to find rates like speed or cost per item. Understand the algebraic and graphical representations of direct proportion (straight lines passing through the origin) and inverse proportion (curved graphs where one variable increases as the other decreases).

core.h: 1. Introduction to Gradient as Rate of Change
core.p: In real-life linear graphs, the gradient is never just a number; it represents a rate of change. This means it shows how one variable changes with respect to another, complete with compound units like metres per second or pounds per hour.
bullets: The **rate of change** measures how fast one quantity changes compared to another.
On a graph, it is calculated as the vertical change divided by the horizontal change.
The formula is Gradient = Change in vertical axis / Change in horizontal axis.
Units for the gradient are always expressed as (vertical unit) per (horizontal unit).

callouts.p: Always include compound units in your final answer for a rate of change (e.g., miles/hour, cm/week).

core.h: 2. Calculating Gradient from a Straight-Line Graph
core.p: To find the rate of change from a straight-line graph, you must select two points on the line and form a right-angled triangle. Drawing a clear, large triangle helps minimize reading errors from the grid lines.
bullets: Identify coordinates (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) on the line.
Calculate the vertical rise: y2 - y1.
Calculate the horizontal run: x2 - x1.
Divide the rise by the run to find the gradient.

callouts.p: Pick points where the line crosses grid intersections exactly to make subtraction easy.

fig.cap: Calculating the gradient of a straight-line graph using a right-angled triangle.

core.p: Real-world graphs link physical quantities. Understanding the axes helps you translate the mathematical gradient into a practical meaning.
bullets: If distance is on the vertical axis and time is on the horizontal axis, the gradient is **speed**.
If total cost is on the vertical axis and number of items is on the horizontal axis, the gradient is **unit cost**.
If water volume is on the vertical axis and time is on the horizontal axis, the gradient is **flow rate**.
A steeper line indicates a faster rate of change.

callouts.p: The speed at which a variable changes over a specific period of time or distance.

core.p: Two quantities are in direct proportion if, as one increases, the other increases at a constant rate. Crucially, when one is zero, the other is also zero, meaning the graph starts at the origin.
bullets: Algebraically written as y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.
As x doubles, y also doubles.
The ratio y / x is always equal to k.
Examples include total pay based on hours worked at a fixed hourly rate.

callouts.p: A direct proportion graph must be a straight line that passes directly through (0, 0).

core.p: The graphical representation of direct proportion is straightforward and easy to spot in an exam. Recognizing this shape allows you to confirm proportional relationships instantly.
bullets: The graph is a straight line.
It passes through the origin (0, 0).
The constant of proportionality k is equal to the gradient of the line.
Any point (x, y) on the line can be used to find k by calculating y / x.

callouts.p: If a straight line does not pass through (0, 0), it represents linear growth, NOT direct proportion.

fig.cap: A direct proportion graph is a straight line through the origin.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="50" y2="40" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="320" y2="60" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><text x="330" y="205" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x</text><text x="35" y="35" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">y</text><text x="35" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">0</text><text x="220" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">y = kx</text></svg>

core.p: Two quantities are in inverse proportion if, as one increases, the other decreases at a proportional rate. Their product always remains constant.
bullets: Algebraically written as y = k / x or xy = k, where k is the constant of proportionality.
As x is multiplied by 3, y is divided by 3.
Examples include the time taken to complete a job and the number of workers assigned to it.

callouts.p: In inverse proportion, multiplying any corresponding x and y values always gives the exact same constant k.

core.p: Unlike direct proportion, inverse proportion produces a curve rather than a straight line. This curve demonstrates a decreasing rate of change that approaches the axes without ever touching them.
bullets: The graph is a curved line called a rectangular hyperbola.
It slopes downwards from left to right.
It gets closer and closer to both the x-axis and y-axis but never touches or crosses them (asymptotes).
Higher values of k shift the curve further away from the origin.

callouts.p: Never connect points of an inverse proportion relationship with a ruler; always sketch a smooth curve.

fig.cap: An inverse proportion graph is a downward-sloping curve.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="50" y2="40" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 70 60 Q 120 180 320 190" fill="none" stroke="#9333ea" stroke-width="3"/><text x="330" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x</text><text x="35" y="35" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">y</text><text x="35" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">0</text><text x="160" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#9333ea">y = k / x</text></svg>

core.p: To solve proportion problems completely, you must find the numerical value of k using given coordinate pairs.
bullets: For direct proportion (y = kx), rearrange to k = y / x.
For inverse proportion (y = k / x), rearrange to k = x multiplied by y.
Substitute the value of k back into the general equation to form your working formula.

callouts.p: Once you find k, write out the complete equation (e.g., y = 5x) before answering further parts of the question.

core.p: Recognizing the differences between direct and inverse proportion is vital for selecting the correct mathematical operation in exam questions.
bullets: Direct: as x goes up, y goes up. Equation: y = kx. Graph: straight line through origin.
Inverse: as x goes up, y goes down. Equation: y = k / x. Graph: curve approaching axes.

core.h: 10. Interpreting Rates of Change in Context
core.p: Exam questions often present graphs tracking journeys, filling tanks, or heating objects, requiring you to interpret gradients at specific sections.
bullets: A horizontal line (gradient = 0) means the quantity is stationary or constant over time.
A steeper positive gradient indicates a faster rate of increase.
A negative gradient indicates a decrease over time (e.g., cooling or emptying).

callouts.p: Gradient: The measure of the steepness of a graph, calculated as vertical change divided by horizontal change.

analogy.t: The Car Journey and Worker Crew Analogy
analogy.p: Think of direct proportion like driving a car at a steady speed: double the time you drive, and you double the distance covered. Think of inverse proportion like painting a fence: double the number of workers on the crew, and the time required to finish is cut in half. This breaks down if workers get in each other's way or stop for breaks, but mathematically the inverse relationship assumes constant efficiency.

terms.d: A measure of how one quantity changes in relation to another quantity.
The steepness of a line, calculated as the change in the vertical coordinate divided by the change in the horizontal coordinate.
A relationship between two quantities where an increase in one leads to a proportional increase in the other, represented by y = kx.
A relationship where an increase in one quantity leads to a proportional decrease in the other, represented by y = k / x.
The multiplier (denoted by k) that relates proportional quantities.
The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis intersect on a Cartesian grid.
A straight-line graph representing a constant rate of change.
The curved graphical shape produced by an inverse proportion relationship.
A line that a graph gets closer and closer to without ever touching.
A unit made by combining two or more units, such as miles per hour or grams per cubic centimetre.
The vertical distance between two points when calculating a gradient.
The horizontal distance between two points when calculating a gradient.

mistakes.w: Saying a graph shows direct proportion because it is a straight line.
mistakes.r: It must be a straight line that passes strictly through the origin (0, 0).

mistakes.w: Calculating gradient as horizontal change divided by vertical change.
mistakes.r: Gradient is always vertical change divided by horizontal change (Rise / Run).

mistakes.w: Writing the inverse proportion equation as y = kx.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion is y = k / x or xy = k.

mistakes.w: Forgetting compound units for a rate of change.
mistakes.r: Always include both units separated by 'per' or a slash (e.g., litres/min).

mistakes.w: Connecting inverse proportion points with straight line segments using a ruler.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion graphs must be drawn as smooth curves.

mistakes.w: Multiplying instead of dividing when finding k for direct proportion.
mistakes.r: For y = kx, find k by doing y divided by x.

exam.q: The graph shows the cost of hiring a plumber. Find the rate of change of cost per hour.
model: Identifies correct coordinates or uses a triangle on the line (1)
exam.tip: Read values carefully from grid intersections and include units.

exam.q: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 4, y = 28. Find the equation connecting y and x.
exam.tip: Substitute the given values into y = kx to find k first.

exam.q: y is inversely proportional to x. When x = 2, y = 10. Find the value of y when x = 5.
exam.tip: For inverse proportion, multiply x and y to find k.

exam.q: Explain how to tell from a graph whether two variables are in direct proportion.
model: Must state the graph is a straight line (1)
Must state it passes through the origin (0, 0) (1)
exam.tip: Both conditions must be mentioned to secure both marks.

exam.q: A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. What is the gradient of the distance-time graph for this journey?
exam.tip: Distance is vertical and time is horizontal on distance-time graphs.

exam.q: The time (t minutes) to fill a pool is inversely proportional to the number of pipes (n). 4 pipes take 30 minutes. Find the time taken by 6 pipes.
exam.tip: Check if your answer makes sense: more pipes should take less time.

exam.q: A straight line has equation y = 3x + 5. Does this represent direct proportion? Explain your answer.
model: Explains that when x = 0, y = 5, so it does not pass through the origin (1)
exam.tip: The +5 intercept ruins direct proportion.

exam.q: Find the constant of proportionality k if y is directly proportional to x and y = 36 when x = 9.
exam.tip: Keep working clear and show division.

exam.q: Sketch the graph of y = 12 / x for positive values of x.
model: Shows curve approaching both axes without touching them (1)
exam.tip: Ensure the line is curved and never touches the axes.

exam.q: The graph of weight against volume for a metal bar is a straight line through the origin. What does the gradient represent?
exam.tip: Recall compound units spec points: mass divided by volume is density.

worked.q: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 6, y = 42. (a) Find the equation connecting y and x. (b) Find y when x = 11.
steps: Write down the general equation for direct proportion: y = kx.
Substitute the given values into the equation to find k: 42 = k * 6.
Solve for k: k = 42 / 6 = 7.
Write the final formula: y = 7x.
Substitute x = 11 into the formula: y = 7 * 11.
Calculate the final answer: y = 77.

worked.q: p is inversely proportional to q. When p = 4, q = 8. (a) Find the formula for p in terms of q. (b) Find p when q = 16.
steps: Write down the general equation for inverse proportion: p = k / q.
Substitute the given values to find k: 4 = k / 8.
Solve for k by multiplying: k = 4 * 8 = 32.
Write the formula: p = 32 / q.
Substitute q = 16 into the formula: p = 32 / 16.
Calculate the final answer: p = 2.

maths_aqa_f.2.12.summary: Inverse proportion describes a relationship where as one variable increases, the other variable decreases at a constant rate, meaning their product remains a constant value. At Foundation tier, students must understand this relationship expressed as proportion to 1/Y, set up algebraic equations using a constant of proportionality k, and interpret them in practical contexts such as time and speed problems.

core.p: Inverse proportion happens when two variables move in opposite directions. If you double one variable, the other variable is halved. If you triple one, the other is divided by three. Their product always stays exactly the same.
bullets: As $X$ increases, $Y$ decreases.
As $X$ decreases, $Y$ increases.
The product of the two variables ($X \times Y$) is always a constant value.
Commonly seen in real life: fewer workers mean it takes more time to build a wall.

callouts.p: A relationship between two variables where an increase in one variable results in a proportional decrease in the other variable.

fig.cap: A conceptual view showing that as workers increase, the time required decreases while the total worker-hours remain constant.

core.p: In mathematics, we use the proportionality symbol to show how variables relate. When $X$ is inversely proportional to $Y$, we write $X$ is proportional to $1 / Y$. This fractional form is the exact definition required by the AQA specification.
bullets: The symbol for proportionality is written as a sideways fish or alpha shape.
Inverse proportion is written as X is proportional to 1 over Y.
It means $X$ varies directly with the reciprocal of $Y$.
Never write $X$ is proportional to $-Y$; inverse means reciprocal, not negative.

callouts.p: X \propto \frac{1}{Y}$ means X is inversely proportional to Y.

core.p: To turn a proportional statement into a useful algebraic equation, we remove the proportionality sign and replace it with an equals sign and a constant multiplier, usually called $k$. This allows us to calculate exact values for any given input.
bullets: Replace the proportionality sign with $= k \times$
The equation becomes $X = \frac{k}{Y}$
Alternatively, multiplying both sides by $Y$ gives $X \times Y = k$
The letter $k$ represents the constant product of the two variables.

callouts.p: The fixed value $k$ that relates two inversely proportional variables, found by multiplying $X$ and $Y$ together.

core.p: Exam questions almost always provide a pair of corresponding values for $X$ and $Y$. You must use these initial numbers to calculate the value of the constant $k$ before doing anything else.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the general equation $X = \frac{k}{Y}$ or $XY = k$.
Step 2: Substitute the given numbers into your equation.
Step 3: Solve the equation to find the value of $k$.
Step 4: Rewrite the full equation with your numerical value for $k$.

callouts.p: Writing out the formula with your calculated $k$ value (e.g. $XY = 60$) earns method marks even if you make an arithmetic error later.

core.p: Constructing an equation means taking information given in a word problem and translating it into mathematical symbols. You must identify which variable takes the place of $X$ and which takes the place of $Y$.
bullets: Read carefully to see which letter depends on the other.
If time $T$ is inversely proportional to speed $S$, write $T = \frac{k}{S}$.
Be careful with letter choices given in the exam question; use their letters.
Constructing the equation correctly is worth the first 1 or 2 marks.

core.p: Once you have constructed and solved your equation, you must interpret what the numbers mean in the context of the real-world problem. This includes finding missing values and explaining real-life constraints.
bullets: Substitute a new value for one variable to find the other.
Check that your answer makes logical sense in context.
If workers increase, check that the time decreases.
Include correct units in your final answer when specified.

core.p: Understanding that $1 / Y$ is the reciprocal of $Y$ is vital for Foundation tier students aiming for top grades. As $Y$ gets larger, $1 / Y$ gets smaller, which pulls $X$ down with it.
bullets: The reciprocal of 2 is 1 over 2 (0.5).
The reciprocal of 5 is 1 over 5 (0.2).
As the denominator $Y$ grows, the fraction $1/Y$ shrinks towards zero.
This explains why inverse proportion curves approach the axes without touching them.

core.p: In calculator and non-calculator papers, examiners may give you a table of values and ask if they show inverse proportion. You must test whether the product of the two variables is constant across every column.
bullets: Multiply every $X$ value by its corresponding $Y$ value.
If $X \times Y$ gives the exact same number every time, it is inverse proportion.
If the products differ even once, the variables are not inversely proportional.
Do not rely on looking at patterns; always multiply to check.

callouts.p: For inverse proportion, XY must be constant. Here 2x30 = 4x15 = 5x12 = 10x6 = 60.

core.p: Unlike direct proportion which forms a straight line through the origin, inverse proportion produces a curve called a hyperbola. The curve starts high on the vertical axis and sweeps down towards the horizontal axis.
bullets: The graph slopes downwards from left to right.
It is curved, not straight.
The line never touches the x-axis or y-axis because $Y$ can never equal zero.
As $X$ gets very large, $Y$ gets very close to zero.

core.p: The most frequent context for inverse proportion in AQA exams involves people completing a task, such as builders painting a house or machines packing boxes. More workers mean fewer hours required.
bullets: Assume every worker works at the exact same rate unless stated otherwise.
Total worker-hours or worker-days remains constant ($k$).
Multiply number of workers by number of hours to find $k$.
Divide $k$ by the new number of workers to find the new time.

callouts.p: Students often think if 4 workers take 6 hours, 2 workers take 3 hours. That is direct proportion! Fewer workers take MORE time.

core.h: 11. Common Contexts: Speed and Journey Time
core.p: Another standard AQA context is travel. If you travel a fixed distance, increasing your speed decreases the time it takes to complete the journey.
bullets: Distance is the constant $k$ in speed-time problems.
Equation: Time = Distance / Speed, or Time is proportional to 1 / Speed.
Doubling your speed cuts your journey time in half.
Always check your speed and time units match (e.g., hours and mph).

core.p: AQA multi-mark proportion questions follow a strict structure. Securing full marks requires writing down the general proportionality relation, inserting $k$, finding $k$ using given values, writing the completed formula, and finally substituting the new value.
bullets: Step 1: Write proportionality statement (1 mark).
Step 2: Form equation with $k$ and substitute to find $k$ (1-2 marks).
Step 3: State completed formula (1 mark).
Step 4: Substitute final values and calculate answer (1 mark).

callouts.p: Does your final number make sense? If speed went up, time must go down. If it didn't, recheck your division.

analogy.p: Imagine a see-saw balanced on a pivot. If you move a heavy child closer to the center, you need to push down with more force, or if you balance weight on a beam, as one side goes up, the other must go down. In inverse proportion, one variable is like weight and the other is distance from the pivot: as one goes up, the other must go down so their product (torque) stays balanced. Where this breaks down: a see-saw is linear and additive, whereas inverse proportion involves multiplication and a curved hyperbolic relationship.

mistakes.w: Writing X = kY instead of X = k / Y for inverse proportion.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion requires dividing by Y, so X = k / Y or XY = k.

mistakes.w: Using addition or subtraction instead of multiplication to find k.
mistakes.r: The constant k is always found by multiplying X and Y together (k = XY).

mistakes.w: Assuming that if workers halve, time halves.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion means fewer workers take more time (time doubles).

mistakes.w: Drawing a straight line for an inverse proportion graph.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion graphs are always curves (hyperbolas), never straight lines.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write the final equation with the numerical value of k.
mistakes.r: You must state the equation with k evaluated before answering subsequent parts.

mistakes.w: Thinking k changes as X and Y change.
mistakes.r: The constant k never changes for a given problem; it remains fixed.

mistakes.w: Writing Y proportional to X instead of 1/Y.
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion to Y is written as proportional to 1/Y.

B) y = k / x

exam.tip: Inverse proportion always has the constant divided by the variable.

exam.q: A car travelling at 60 mph takes 3 hours to complete a journey. How long will it take at 90 mph?
exam.tip: Speed and time are inversely proportional. Distance is your constant k.

exam.tip: Show working for every pair to prove the product is identical.

exam.q: m is inversely proportional to n. When n = 5, m = 8. Find the value of n when m = 20.
exam.tip: Set up the equation using k = 40, then substitute the new m value.

exam.q: Complete the statement: y is inversely proportional to x can be written as y is proportional to ...
exam.tip: Know the exact specification phrasing: proportion to 1/Y.

worked.q:
y is inversely proportional to x. When x = 5, y = 8.
(a) Find an equation linking x and y.
(b) Calculate the value of y when x = 10.
(c) Calculate the value of x when y = 2.
steps: Write the general inverse proportion equation: y = k / x
Substitute x = 5 and y = 8 into the equation: 8 = k / 5
Solve for k by multiplying both sides by 5: k = 8 x 5 = 40
State the final equation: y = 40 / x
For part (b), substitute x = 10: y = 40 / 10 = 4
For part (c), substitute y = 2: 2 = 40 / x, so x = 40 / 2 = 20

worked.q:
5 machines can finish an order in 12 days. Assuming all machines work at the same rate:
(a) Set up a proportion equation where M is machines and D is days.
(b) How many days will it take 3 machines?
steps: Recognise that machines and days are inversely proportional: M is proportional to 1 / D, or M x D = k.
Calculate k using 5 machines and 12 days: k = 5 x 12 = 60.
Construct the equation: M x D = 60 or D = 60 / M.
For part (b), substitute M = 3 into the equation: D = 60 / 3.
Calculate the final answer: D = 20.

maths_aqa_f.2.14.summary: Master growth and decay problems for Foundation tier AQA GCSE Mathematics by learning how to repeatedly apply percentage multipliers. You will explore compound interest for savings and loans, calculate depreciating asset values over time, and understand how iterative processes use step-by-step repeating calculations to find approximate solutions.

core.p: Growth and decay problems involve quantities that increase or decrease by a percentage over equal time intervals. Unlike simple interest which adds the same flat amount every year, compound growth and decay apply the percentage change to the updated amount from the previous period.
bullets: Growth means a quantity increases repeatedly over time, such as money in a bank account earning interest or a bacteria population multiplying.
Decay means a quantity decreases repeatedly over time, such as the value of a car depreciating or medicine leaving the bloodstream.
Repeated percentage changes cannot be calculated by adding or subtracting the percentages together; you must use multiplicative growth factors.
Every growth or decay problem relies on setting up a starting amount and a multiplier raised to a power representing time periods.

callouts.p: Always convert percentages into decimal multipliers before applying powers for time.

core.p: To work with compound growth and decay efficiently, you must convert percentages into decimal multipliers. The multiplier represents the proportion of the original amount that remains or is added after each specific time period.
bullets: For percentage growth, add the percentage to 100%, then divide by 100 to get a decimal greater than 1.
Example: An increase of 5% gives 100% + 5% = 105%, which converts to the multiplier 1.05.
Example: An increase of 23% gives 100% + 23% = 123%, which converts to the multiplier 1.23.
For percentage decay, subtract the percentage from 100%, then divide by 100 to get a decimal less than 1.
Example: A decrease of 12% gives 100% - 12% = 88%, which converts to the multiplier 0.88.
Example: A decrease of 6.5% gives 100% - 6.5% = 93.5%, which converts to the multiplier 0.935.

callouts.p: If your multiplier is greater than 1, it represents growth. If it is less than 1, it represents decay.

core.p: Compound interest is added to the principal amount and also to the accumulated interest of previous periods. This creates exponential growth where the amount added grows larger every single year.
bullets: The standard formula is Final Value = Principal multiplied by (Multiplier raised to the power of time).
Written algebraically as: Total = P times (1 + r/100) to the power of n, where P is principal, r is percentage rate, and n is number of years.
The principal is the initial amount of money invested or borrowed.
The power n represents the number of compounding periods, usually years.
Examiners often award method marks for correctly identifying the multiplier and the power before you calculate the final answer.

callouts.p: Interest calculated on the initial principal and also on the accumulated interest of previous periods of a deposit or loan.

core.p: When solving compound interest questions in the calculator paper, you should write down the exact formula substitution first, then evaluate using your calculator, and finally round appropriately for money.
bullets: Step 1: Identify the starting amount (Principal).
Step 2: Calculate the decimal multiplier for the given interest rate.
Step 3: Write down the calculation with the time period as the power.
Step 4: Enter the expression into your calculator in one smooth step.
Step 5: Round money answers to the nearest penny (2 decimal places) unless the question instructs otherwise.

callouts.p: Never round intermediate numbers during multi-step calculations. Only round your final recorded answer.

core.p: Depreciation is the reduction in the value of an asset over time, such as a car, machinery, or electronic equipment. It is calculated using the exact same multiplier method as compound interest, but with a multiplier less than 1.
bullets: If a car depreciates by 15% per year, its value each year is 85% of the previous year's value.
The multiplier for a 15% depreciation is 0.85.
To find the value after 4 years, multiply the original price by 0.85 to the power of 4.
Depreciation curves drop steeply at first because 15% of a large initial price is a bigger cash drop than 15% of a smaller future price.
Always check whether the question asks for the total depreciation (drop in value) or the final remaining value.

callouts.p: Total Depreciation = Original Value minus Final Value. Read carefully to give what the examiner asks for!

core.p: Sometimes exam questions give you the final value after growth or decay and ask you to work backwards to find the original starting amount. This requires setting up an equation and solving for the unknown principal.
bullets: Let the unknown original amount be x.
Set up the equation: x multiplied by (multiplier to the power of time) equals the final value.
To solve for x, divide the final value by the multiplier raised to the power.
Alternative algebraic method: x times multiplier to the power = Final Value, so x = Final Value divided by (multiplier to the power n).
Never try to divide the final value first and then apply the power; always isolate x properly using inverse operations.

callouts.p: Students often mistakenly multiply the final value by the multiplier instead of dividing when working backwards.

core.h: Finding the Number of Time Periods (Powers)
core.p: Foundation tier candidates may encounter problems where the time period (the power n) is unknown, though usually solved by trial and improvement or systematic testing on your calculator.
bullets: If an investment starts at 1000 pounds and grows by 5% per year with multiplier 1.05, how many years until it exceeds 1300 pounds?
Test integer values for the power n systematically.
Try n = 5: 1000 times (1.05 to the power of 5) = 1276.28 pounds (not enough).
Try n = 6: 1000 times (1.05 to the power of 6) = 1340.10 pounds (exceeds 1300 pounds).
Conclude that it takes 6 full years for the investment to cross the target threshold.

callouts.p: Always write down at least one trial calculation that is too low and one that is too high to secure full marks.

core.p: An iterative process is a repetitive mathematical procedure where the output of one calculation becomes the input for the next calculation. Each repetition brings you closer and closer to an accurate solution.
bullets: Iteration uses a recurrence relation, usually written with subscript notation like x subscript (n+1) in terms of x subscript n.
You are almost always given a starting value, labeled x subscript 0.
Substitute x subscript 0 into the formula to find the first generated value, x subscript 1.
Substitute x subscript 1 into the formula to find x subscript 2, and continue for the number of iterations requested.
Always write down every intermediate decimal value clearly to avoid losing accuracy marks.

callouts.p: The repetition of a process in order to generate a sequence of outcomes designed to approach a target value or root.

core.p: When answering exam questions on iteration, examiners expect you to lay out your working clearly, showing each step subscript by subscript. Modern calculators have built-in memory features that make this extremely fast.
bullets: Example rule: x subscript (n+1) = square root of (10 - 2 times x subscript n), with x subscript 0 = 2.
Find x subscript 1: square root of (10 - 2 times 2) = square root of 6 = 2.44949...
Find x subscript 2: square root of (10 - 2 times 2.44949) = square root of 5.10101... = 2.25854...
Find x subscript 3: square root of (10 - 2 times 2.25854) = square root of 5.48291... = 2.34156...
Always record decimals to the degree of accuracy requested in the question, often 3 or 4 decimal places.

callouts.p: Type your starting value, press equals, then type the formula using the Ans button to repeat instantly.

core.p: Iteration is a powerful numerical method used to find approximate solutions to equations that cannot be easily solved using standard algebraic rearrangement.
bullets: An equation like x cubed + x = 10 can be rearranged into iterative formulas like x = cube root of (10 - x).
The sequence of values generated by the iteration converges toward the exact root of the equation.
Convergence means the numbers get closer and closer to a stable value where further iterations do not change the decimal places.
If the numbers start flying off to infinity or alternating wildly between two values, the iteration is said to diverge.
Foundation questions will guide you step-by-step through the rearrangement and the first few calculated values.

callouts.p: When successive iterations produce the same value to a given decimal place, you have found the approximate root.

core.h: Financial Maths Contexts: Savings and Loans
core.p: Compound interest appears frequently in real-world financial contexts involving bank savings accounts, mortgages, and hire purchase agreements.
bullets: Savings accounts pay compound interest, meaning your balance increases faster as the years pass because you earn interest on previous interest.
Loans and credit cards often charge compound interest, meaning the debt grows exponentially if only minimum payments are made.
AER (Annual Equivalent Rate) tells you the actual interest rate earned over a full year taking compound compounding frequency into account.
Always check whether interest is compounded annually (once a year) or monthly, though Foundation tier almost exclusively tests annual compounding.

callouts.p: Never use simple interest methods (multiplying annual interest by years and adding on) unless the question explicitly states 'simple interest'.

core.h: Exam Strategy for Growth and Decay
core.p: Securing top marks in growth, decay, and iteration questions requires disciplined working out and careful reading of command words.
bullets: Check if the question asks for the total final amount or just the interest/depreciation earned or lost.
Write down the multiplier explicitly as your first line of working to pick up method marks even if calculator keystrokes fail.
Pay meticulous attention to rounding instructions such as 'give your answer to the nearest penny' or 'to 3 decimal places'.
In iteration questions, ensure you write down every single requested term (x1, x2, x3) clearly labelled.

callouts.p: Include pound signs for financial answers and ensure units match throughout multi-part problems.

analogy.t: The Snowball Rolling Down a Hill
analogy.p: Compound growth is like a snowball rolling down a snowy hill. As it rolls, it picks up more snow. Because it is now bigger, every rotation picks up even more snow than the last rotation, making it grow faster and faster. Simple interest is like adding a fixed cup of snow every minute regardless of how big the snowball is. The analogy breaks down because real snowballs eventually hit physical limits in size, whereas mathematical compound growth continues exponentially forever.

The reduction in the value of an asset over a period of time.
A decimal number used to scale an amount up or down to represent a percentage increase or decrease.

Growth whose rate becomes increasingly rapid in proportion to the growing total number or size.
The repetition of a mathematical process to generate a sequence of outcomes approaching a target value.
An equation that defines each term of a sequence using preceding terms.
The tendency of a sequence of iterative numbers to approach a stable limiting value.
An increase in the monetary value of an asset over time.
The decimal multiplier greater than 1 used to calculate repeated percentage increases.
The decimal multiplier less than 1 used to calculate repeated percentage decreases.
A solution to an equation, often found numerically using iterative methods.

mistakes.w: Adding the percentage increase to the total each year as a flat amount (treating it like simple interest).
mistakes.r: Recognise that compound interest applies the percentage to the new updated total every year.

mistakes.w: Using a multiplier of 1.5 for a 5% increase or 0.15 for a 15% decrease.
mistakes.r: Convert 5% increase to 1.05 and 15% decrease to 0.85.

mistakes.w: Multiplying the principal by the time power first before applying the multiplier.
mistakes.r: Apply the order of operations: the power applies strictly and only to the multiplier.

mistakes.w: Dividing the final value by the multiplier when trying to find forward compound interest.
mistakes.r: Multiplication is for going forward in time; division is only for working backwards to find the original amount.

mistakes.w: Stopping an iteration table early without calculating all requested terms like x1, x2, and x3.
mistakes.r: Read the question carefully and write down every required step subscript by subscript.

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate calculator numbers to 1 decimal place halfway through a compound interest problem.
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer line, then round appropriately.

mistakes.w: Stating that a depreciation multiplier of 0.8 means a depreciation of 0.8%.
mistakes.r: A multiplier of 0.8 represents 80% remaining, which means a 20% decrease.

exam.q: Aleena invests 4000 pounds in a savings account paying 3% compound interest per year. Work out the total amount in the account after 2 years.
exam.tip: Write down your multiplier and power clearly before evaluating.

exam.q: A car has a value of 12000 pounds. It depreciates by 15% each year. Find its value after 3 years.
exam.tip: Depreciation uses a multiplier less than 1.

exam.q: The value of a painting increases by 4% every year. The painting is worth 5000 pounds now. What will it be worth in 5 years? Give your answer to the nearest pound.

worked.q: A digital camera depreciates in value by 18% each year. When new, it cost 450 pounds. Find the value of the camera after 3 years. Give your answer to the nearest penny.
steps: Identify the original value: 450 pounds.
Calculate the decimal multiplier for an 18% decrease: 100% - 18% = 82%, which is 0.82.
Set up the compound decay calculation: 450 x (0.82 cubed).
Evaluate the expression: 450 x 0.5513688 = 248.11596 pounds.
Round to 2 decimal places: 248.12 pounds.

worked.q: Use the iteration formula x subscript (n+1) = 2 over (x subscript n squared) + 1, starting with x subscript 0 = 1.5, to find x subscript 1, x subscript 2, and x subscript 3. Give your answers to 4 decimal places.
steps: For x1, substitute x0 = 1.5 into the formula: 2 / (1.5 squared) + 1 = 2 / 2.25 + 1 = 0.88888 + 1 = 1.8889.
For x2, substitute x1 = 1.88888... into the formula: 2 / (1.88888 squared) + 1 = 2 / 3.5679 + 1 = 1.5606.
For x3, substitute x2 = 1.5606... into the formula: 2 / (1.5606 squared) + 1 = 2 / 2.4355 + 1 = 1.8213.
Ensure all answers are clearly stated to 4 decimal places.
